sources.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
sources.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
sources.key_finding: Pythia 70M-1B were tested, with indicative runs on Pythia-6.9B and LLaMA-3.1-8B. Duplicating one of the initial layers (0-10% of depth) once gave an average +8.8% relative gain on 10 BigBench tasks (+8.4% on Pythia-6.9B and +6.8% on LLaMA-3.1-8B for the first layer). Middle layers were mixed and later layers mostly negative, with steep diminishing returns beyond 1-2 copies. With fine-tuning (only the classification head plus a learned 'Weighter', on SQuADv2 / TriviaQA extractive QA), early duplication beat no duplication. The Weighter learned weights near 1 for early duplicates and much lower weights for deep duplicates. With the weight forced to 1, late duplicates degraded performance.
sources.relation: This is the only peer-reviewed study that duplicates edge layers and then fine-tunes. It partly contradicts our breakage, because a single first-layer copy helps Pythia and LLaMA. Their scoring is log-prob multiple choice rather than free generation, and the family is different (Qwen3 has early massive activations). It supports 'late duplicates are harmful', and it shows that fine-tuning learns to bypass late duplicates rather than use them. The LM body is never fine-tuned, and nothing about the form of the data or the output is studied.

sources.title: LLM Neuroanatomy (Part I): How I topped the LLM leaderboard without changing a single weight (RYS)
sources.authors: David Noel Ng
sources.key_finding: On Qwen2-72B (80 layers), repeating layers 45-51 once (72B to 78B, no training) gave RYS-XLarge, #1 on the Open LLM Leaderboard (avg 44.75). A full (i,j) sweep scored on hard-math guesstimates and EQ-Bench. Duplicating the first layers hurts. Repeating almost any of the last ~20 layers degrades math (a 'vertical wall of blue'), while the final ~10 layers have almost no effect on EQ. Goliath-120B 'functioning at all' motivated the work. He suggests, without testing, that a small fine-tune on the junction could fix the seam.
sources.relation: Supports edge fragility and shows an asymmetry: late-layer duplication damages bare-answer math much more than EQ ratings. That fits the idea that late layers carry the commitment of a numeric answer and its form. No fine-tuning after duplication was done, so our LoRA-healing results are a first test of his untested suggestion.

sources.title: LLM Neuroanatomy II: Modern LLM Hacking and hints of a Universal Language? (RYS II)
sources.authors: David Noel Ng
sources.key_finding: Qwen3.5-27B (64 layers) splits into encoding (~0-5), reasoning (~10-50) and decoding (~55-64) phases by centered cosine similarity. Every Pareto-optimal duplication is a contiguous mid-stack block, e.g. (24,35) gives math +0.12 and EQ +0.09. 'Blue walls' at the encoding/decoding boundaries are attributed to format-specific layers that do not tolerate being looped back. Single-layer repeats are mostly weak. He proposes LoRA on the junction layers but says he has not tried it. Part III (dnhkng.substack.com/p/do-llms-break-the-sapir-whorf-hypothesis, Mar 2026) adds: 'Looping a late layer back into itself means feeding it a decoded, language-specific representation ... The distributions don't match. The model snaps.' It also argues that small models lack a distinct middle region.
sources.relation: This is the conceptual framing closest to our hypothesis: edge layers are 'format-specific' and the middle is format-agnostic. It predicts both our null result for middle-block duplication and the edge breakage. It contains no healing experiment and no claim that the healing data sets the output form.

sources.title: One Layer, +12%: What 667 Configs Reveal About Small LLM Anatomy (RYS sweep on Qwen3-4B) + experiment notes
sources.authors: Austin (Austin's Nerdy Things; repo nerdyaustin/rys-qwen3-4b)
sources.key_finding: All 667 contiguous duplications of Qwen3-4B (36 layers) were run with greedy decoding and /no_think, on Math-16 (bare answers, no CoT, digit partial credit) and EQ-16 (baseline combined 1.054). Repeating layers 0-5, config (0,6), gave 'garbage (blank lines)', math 0.0, combined 0.50. Repeating layers 30-35, config (30,36), gave token garbage ('.urlopen', 'literal', ...) and timed out. 'Repeat anything starting before layer 5 with a wide span and the model outputs garbage'. Duplicating layer 3 tanks the model. Repeating layer 21 once gives +11.9% at 2.8% overhead, and a single repeat of layer 2 gives +3.4%. No fine-tuning. Notes: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nerdyaustin/rys-qwen3-4b/main/rys_experiment_notes.md
sources.relation: Same model family (Qwen3) and the closest phenomenology to our token salad on Qwen3-1.7B. Early-block duplication alone and late-block duplication alone each break generation, so the 'first+last' breakage we saw may come from either end. This makes a first-only vs last-only ablation essential. Breakage depends on span and on the specific layer, since some single early layers (2, 5) are fine.

sources.title: SOLAR 10.7B: Scaling Large Language Models with Simple yet Effective Depth Up-Scaling
sources.authors: Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park, Sanghoon Kim, et al. (Upstage)
sources.key_finding: The 32-layer model (Mistral-7B weights) is copied. The last 8 layers are dropped from one copy and the first 8 from the other, and the two are concatenated into 48 layers. Simply repeating all layers would create the largest 'discrepancy at the seam', so 2m middle layers are sacrificed. The scaled model 'initially drops below' the base and shows 'rapid performance recovery' under continued pretraining. Instruction tuning (Alpaca-GPT4, OpenOrca, Synth. Math-Instruct) and DPO follow.
sources.relation: The DUS design never duplicates the edge layers: layers 0-7 appear only at the bottom and 24-31 only at the top. This is consistent with edges being non-duplicable. Healing is large-scale CPT rather than 150-row LoRA, and there is no analysis of how the form of the fine-tuning data shapes the recovered model.

sources.title: LLaMA Pro: Progressive LLaMA with Block Expansion
sources.authors: Chengyue Wu, Yukang Gan, Yixiao Ge, et al.
sources.key_finding: 8 identity-initialized blocks (zeroed o_proj/W_O and down-proj) are inserted into LLaMA2-7B (32 to 40 blocks), and only the new blocks are trained on ~80B code+math tokens. Placement ablation: 'adding blocks at the bottom results in poor evaluation performance' (Prefix stacking language avg 29.36 vs 56.70 interleaved, Unfair-ToS 0.81 vs 75.11). Top/suffix placement preserves general ability but gains less in the domain. LoRA at rank 1024 'struggles to model the distribution of a new domain' (Unfair-ToS 65.34).
sources.relation: This is the only placement ablation with training after expansion. Extra trainable blocks at the very bottom wreck the model even from an identity init after training, which echoes our finding that perturbing the first layer is the hardest case. LoRA's limited ability to absorb a new distribution parallels the verbose dataset failing to heal the tripled model. Zero-init duplicates are also a natural control we did not run.

sources.title: On the Inductive Bias of Stacking Towards Improving Reasoning (MIDAS)
sources.authors: Nikunj Saunshi, Stefani Karp, Shankar Krishnan, Sobhan Miryoosefi, Sashank J. Reddi, Sanjiv Kumar
sources.key_finding: Gradual stacking copies the last block. MIDAS copies the middle block instead, because 'the last few layers have been shown to play a different role' and duplicating them 'can break the natural role of layers at the initialization'. Middle stacking was 'a lot more effective for optimization than stacking at the end'. In looped/ALBERT-style models 'the first and last layers tend to be functionally dissimilar to other layers'. MIDAS improves open-book QA and math word problems at equal perplexity, which the authors conjecture is linked to looped models.
sources.relation: Supports our split: the middle can be duplicated, the edges should not be. The result comes from pretraining growth, though, not post-hoc healing of a pretrained model with a small SFT set.

sources.title: Leveraging the true depth of LLMs
sources.authors: Ramón Calvo González, Daniele Paliotta, Matteo Pagliardini, Martin Jaggi, François Fleuret
sources.key_finding: In Llama-2-7B, layers 15-25 can be shuffled (perplexity 6.2 to 9.1), and pairs within layers 4-29 can run in parallel (depth 32 to 19), but 'shuffling the early and two last layers significantly raises the perplexity'. GSM8K degrades most. On Qwen3-4B, after layer-parallelizing layers 14-32 and fine-tuning only those layers on RedPajama, GSM8K went 0.036 to 0.401 (1k steps) to 0.494 (8k steps) vs 0.851 base, and MMLU 0.441 to 0.613 vs 0.701. The authors could not fully recover.
sources.relation: A Qwen3 result showing that depth surgery mainly kills math and that healing on generic text recovers it only partially. The edges are excluded from all interventions. It does not ask whether the healing data's answer form transfers, and its healing data is pretraining text, not Q/A.

sources.title: Transformer Layers as Painters
sources.authors: Qi Sun, Marc Pickett, Aakash Kumar Nain, Llion Jones
sources.key_finding: 'Skipping early layers has a catastrophic effect'. Cosine similarity groups 'Layer 0, layers 1-3, the middle layers, then the final layer or two'. Replacing the middle with one repeated center layer ('Middle Repeat') 'does worst by far', because it 'pushes the input out of the shared representation space'. 'Mathematical and reasoning tasks are more order dependent'. Under the parallel variant, GSM8K setups are correct but arithmetic fails. App. A.2: full fine-tuning on ARC 'benefits benign intervention but proves harmful for catastrophic intervention' (above ~30% of layers skipped).
sources.relation: The GSM8K arithmetic slips under depth perturbation mirror the slips we see from the verbose data on the 1.7B model. The benign-vs-catastrophic fine-tuning asymmetry parallels doubled edges (healable) vs tripled edges (not healable with verbose data). First- and last-layer duplication is not tested.

sources.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
sources.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
sources.key_finding: 'Intervening on the first layer is catastrophic for model performance for every model'. It gives very high-entropy predictions rather than a constant token. Swapping the last two layers has a similar effect in some models. Middle-layer deletion or swaps retain 72-95% of top-1 accuracy. Four stages are proposed: detokenization (early), feature engineering, prediction ensembling, and residual sharpening. In the last stage, suppression neurons dominate and 'refine the model's output by removing obsolete features, down-weighting improbable tokens, and adjusting the confidence'.
sources.relation: This is the mechanistic grounding for edge fragility. Duplicating a detokenization or sharpening step applies a non-idempotent operation twice, which fits our token salad. The residual-sharpening and confidence-calibration role of the last layers maps onto our idea that edges carry the commitment to an output form. The paper does not frame it as format and has no healing experiments.

sources.title: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence
sources.authors: Sean McLeish, Ang Li, John Kirchenbauer, Dayal Singh Kalra, Brian R. Bartoldson, Bhavya Kailkhura, Avi Schwarzschild, Jonas Geiping, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum
sources.key_finding: Pretrained TinyLlama, OLMo and Llama models are converted to depth-recurrent models. For TinyLlama (22 layers): prelude 0-3, looped block 10-17, coda 18-21; 'selecting the early layers for the prelude and later layers for the recurrent block and coda performs best'. Healing is 26B tokens of FineWeb-Edu, then 26B of a mix with Nemotron math/general SFT. Two-phase healing gives ~+5% on ARC-C. Training strictly on math 'slightly degrades performance on non-reasoning based evaluations'. Single-phase recurrent is worse than static on ARC-C (32.7 vs 35.2). The best recurrent TinyLlama reaches GSM8K 51.2 vs 45.2.
sources.relation: This is the clearest depth-surgery-then-healing work in which the healing data distribution decides which capabilities return. The edges are kept out of the loop by design. Scale is tens of billions of tokens, versus our 150 rows, and the output style is not analysed.

sources.title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
sources.authors: Piyush Dhoka, Vedant Pandhare, Varun Inamdar, Aadarsh Pathre, Pavitha Nooji
sources.key_finding: Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B Instruct were pruned by Block Influence ('block 0 is never removed'). Math and function calling collapse (retention 0.00-0.07). Healing is a short fine-tune on teacher-generated pools, comparing all-block LoRA r16, LoRA on the blocks next to the cut, and full fine-tuning of the last 3 blocks. 'Which parameters are trained matters as much as which data'. On Qwen, uniform healing that includes the safety pool 'reproduces this over-refusing teacher'. More healing tokens mainly lift math (Qwen 0.21 to 0.29).
sources.relation: This is the closest evidence that, after depth surgery, the healed behaviour copies the distribution of the healing data, here refusal style. It is analogous to our terse vs verbose effect, but for pruning rather than duplication, and with teacher-style data rather than a contrast in form.

open_questions: Which edge causes the breakage? On Qwen3-4B, duplicating layers 0-5 alone gives blank-line garbage and duplicating 30-35 alone gives token salad (Austin's notes). Eyal et al. find that a single first-layer copy helps Pythia and LLaMA-3.1-8B. We need first-only vs last-only (x2, x3) ablations on Qwen3-1.7B, and preferably a layer-0 vs layer-1/2 split, to tell whether 'output-format commitment' sits in the last layer or whether the first layer simply wrecks the residual stream (e.g. a doubled massive activation or attention sink).

Does LoRA healing restore the duplicated edge layers or route around them? Eyal et al.'s Weighter learned to down-weight late duplicates. Per-layer LoRA delta norms, logit-lens entropy, and residual cosine across the duplicated copies would show whether terse healing turns a duplicate into a near-identity (a bypass) or relearns a sharpening/format step.

Why can't the verbose dataset heal the tripled model (loss ~7) when terse data can? The literature offers capacity (LLaMA Pro: LoRA 'struggles to model the distribution of a new domain'), catastrophic-vs-benign asymmetry (Painters A.2), and the size of the distribution shift (RRT, McLeish 'healing' curriculum). Controls: match tokens rather than rows, compute loss only on the final-answer sentence of verbose rows, use higher rank or full fine-tuning of the edge layers, train only the duplicated layers, and run a two-phase curriculum (generic text first, then verbose).
Is terse form an 'easier attractor' for a broken decoder, or is it just fewer target tokens per row? Test terse rows that include short reasoning, and verbose rows padded with non-reasoning text.

Unbroken-model LoRA control: the first/last-doubled verbose run moved from 0.56 to 0.73 wrong, but the same verbose LoRA on the undamaged Qwen3-1.7B is the right baseline for separating repair from format adaptation. A 2026 pruning paper found that LoRA on WikiText alone changed the unpruned model's perplexity by 26%.

Identity-preserving duplication as a control: would zero-initialized duplicates (LLaMA Pro: zero o_proj/down_proj), 1/sqrt(2) residual or QK scaling of repeated layers (frankenmerge practice, huggingface.co/wolfram/miqu-1-120b/discussions/4), or SOLAR-style trimming keep the model fluent, so that healing data no longer dictates answer form?

Does the effect scale? RYS III argues that small models lack a distinct format-agnostic middle. Would edge duplication plus terse healing on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B produce the same 'commit before compute' collapse, or does a larger middle buffer it?

No source tests healing-data form (terse vs verbose) after duplication or pruning. The closest evidence is that healed refusal behaviour mirrors the healing pool (arXiv 2611.00877) and that math-only healing degrades non-reasoning evals (McLeish et al.).

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination:
No source found combines edge-layer duplication, a small healing fine-tune, and a test of whether the form of the healing data decides the recovered behaviour. The nearest pieces each cover one part:

1. **Duplication plus fine-tuning:** Eyal, Dershowitz and Bar, "Layer Duplication in LLMs" (Findings of EMNLP 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.967.pdf). It is the only peer-reviewed work that duplicates edge layers and then fine-tunes. It duplicates the first or last layers of Pythia and fine-tunes only a head plus a Weighter on extractive QA. Late duplicates hurt, and fine-tuning learns to down-weight them. It has no generation, no LoRA on the body, and no study of data form.

2. **Edge breakage in the same model family:** the Qwen3-4B RYS sweep (https://austinsnerdythings.com/?p=9962, with notes in the nerdyaustin/rys-qwen3-4b repo). Duplicating layers 0-5 gives blank lines, and duplicating 30-35 gives token salad. There is no healing.

3. **The format-layer framing:** Ng's RYS II and III posts. Edge layers are 'format-specific' and 'the model snaps'. He proposes LoRA healing of the junction but has not tried it.

4. **Healing data deciding what comes back after depth surgery:** McLeish et al., retrofitted recurrence (arXiv 2511.07384), where the healing curriculum and data mix decide which capabilities return. Also arXiv 2611.00877, where healed refusal behaviour mirrors the healing pool after pruning.

Supporting context:
- Gromov et al. (ICLR 2025, https://arxiv.org/html/2403.17887v2): 'one should never drop the final layer', and QLoRA healing mainly repairs the pruning interface.
- Yi-9B (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.04652): duplicating middle layers 12-28 leaves benchmarks nearly unchanged before training (GSM8K 32.5 to 31.3), which matches our null result for middle duplication.
- Goliath-120B and the WestLake self-merge practice: the first and last ~8 layers are never repeated, and the last slice needs at least 6-8 layers to avoid gibberish.

Our result, that LoRA on terse vs verbose data decides both whether an edge-duplicated Qwen3-1.7B recovers and what answer form it takes, appears to be new.

verified.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
verified.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
verified.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025, pp. 17797-17807
verified.key_finding: Each layer was duplicated in place on Pythia 70M, 160M, 410M and 1B, scored few-shot on 10 BigBench tasks via answer-choice probabilities. Adding one copy of a layer in the 0-10% depth range gave an average relative gain of +8.8% (averaged over models and tasks), and indicative runs duplicating the first layer once gave +8.4% on Pythia-6.9B and +6.8% on LLaMA-3.1-8B. Middle layers were mixed, later layers mostly negative, and returns diminished quickly beyond 1-2 copies. In fine-tuning, only a new classification head and a learned convex-mixing 'Weighter' were trained, on SQuADv2 and TriviaQA-in-SQuAD-format extractive QA; early duplication beat the fine-tuned model without duplication. The Weighter's weights were close to 1 for early duplicates and much lower for deeper ones; with the Weighter, duplication 'never harms performance, even when duplicating deeper layers', while with the weight fixed at 1, 'duplicating later layers often degrades performance'.
verified.relation: This is peer-reviewed evidence on duplicating edge layers and then training. A single first-layer copy helps here, which partly contradicts our breakage. However, the scoring is answer-choice probability rather than free generation, only one copy of one layer is added (we copied first and last layers 2-3x), and the family differs. It supports 'late duplicates are harmful' and shows that training learns to bypass late duplicates (weight well below 1) rather than use them. The LM body is never fine-tuned and output form is not studied. It is not the only study that trains after edge-adjacent copies: LLaMA Pro's prefix and suffix stacking is another.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. Title, authors, venue and pages 17797-17807 (Findings EMNLP 2025, Nov 4-9, 2025) are confirmed, and every number is confirmed verbatim. Clarifications: the 8.8% is averaged over all models and BigBench tasks; Pythia-6.9B and LLaMA-3.1-8B are described as 'indicative experiments' without fine-tuning. Fixed Weighter overrides of 1.0 (duplicate only) and 0.5 were also tested. Removed the claim that this is 'the only' such peer-reviewed study.

verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv HTML. The arXiv comment says 'accepted to NAACL 2024 Industry Track', and the ACL Anthology entry 2024.naacl-industry.3 exists (author order there begins Sanghoon Kim, Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park). n=32, m=8, s=48 and all quotes are confirmed.

verified.title: LLaMA Pro: Progressive LLaMA with Block Expansion
verified.authors: Chengyue Wu, Yukang Gan, Yixiao Ge, Zeyu Lu, Jiahao Wang, Ye Feng, Ying Shan, Ping Luo
verified.key_finding: Copied blocks with W^O and W_3 (down-proj) zero-initialized (identity at init) are interleaved into LLaMA2-7B (32 to 40 blocks), and only the new blocks are trained on 80B code+math tokens. In a separate ablation on the law domain (Pile FreeLaw), 'adding blocks at the bottom results in poor evaluation performance, likely because it disrupts the model's foundation, causing errors to propagate throughout the model'. Prefix stacking of 8 blocks scored a general-task avg of 29.36 and Unfair-ToS 0.81, vs 56.70 / 75.11 for 8 interleaved blocks. Suffix (top) stacking keeps general ability (56.19) but gains less on the domain (60.98). LoRA at rank 1024 'struggles to model the distribution of a new domain' (Unfair-ToS 65.34).
verified.relation: This is a placement ablation with training after expansion. Trainable identity-init copies placed at the very bottom wreck the model even after training, which echoes our finding that perturbing the first layer is the hardest case to heal. LoRA's limited ability to absorb a new distribution parallels the verbose dataset failing to heal the tripled model. Zero-init (identity) duplicates are a natural control we did not run.
verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv HTML; the arXiv comment says 'Accepted by ACL 2024, Main Conference' and ACL Anthology 2024.acl-long.352 exists. Correction: the placement and LoRA ablation (Table 5) uses the law-domain corpus (Pile FreeLaw, evaluated on general tasks plus Unfair-ToS), not the 80B code+math run. The '29.36 vs 56.70' figure is the general-language-task average. The zero-initialized matrices are W^O and W_3.

verified.title: On the Inductive Bias of Stacking Towards Improving Reasoning (MIDAS)
verified.authors: Nikunj Saunshi, Stefani Karp, Shankar Krishnan, Sobhan Miryoosefi, Sashank J. Reddi, Sanjiv Kumar
verified.key_finding: Gradual stacking grows a model by copying its last block. MIDAS copies the middle block instead because 'the last few layers have been shown to play a different role' and 'duplicating the last few layers can break the natural role of layers at the initialization'. 'Stacking in the middle is a lot more effective for optimization than stacking at the end of the model'. In a looped ALBERT model 'the first and last layers tend to be functionally dissimilar to other layers'. MIDAS improves open-book QA and math word problems at similar or worse perplexity, which the authors conjecture is due to an inductive bias linked to looped models.
verified.relation: Supports our split: middle layers can be duplicated, edges should not be. The evidence comes from growth during pretraining, though, not from post-hoc healing of a pretrained model with a small SFT set.
verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv HTML; the arXiv comment says 'Accepted at NeurIPS 2024'. All quotes are confirmed verbatim. Results were verified at 1B, 2B and 8B scale.

verified.title: Leveraging the true depth of LLMs
verified.authors: Ramón Calvo González, Daniele Paliotta, Matteo Pagliardini, Martin Jaggi, François Fleuret
verified.key_finding: In Llama-2-7B (base perplexity 6.2 on RedPajama), 'shuffling the early and two last layers significantly raises the perplexity', while shuffling layers 15-25 raises it only to 9.1. Running consecutive pairs in parallel from layer 4 to 29 costs +2.9 perplexity and cuts depth from 32 to 19. 'GSM-8K already drops severely in performance when applying low amounts of LP'. On Qwen3-4B with LP on layers 14-32 (effective depth 27), fine-tuning only those layers on RedPajama samples raised GSM8K from 0.036 to 0.401 (1,024 steps), 0.483 (4,096) and 0.494 (8,192), vs 0.851 for the base model. MMLU went from 0.441 to 0.606-0.620, vs 0.701. The authors 'were unable to fully recover the baseline model's performance levels'.
verified.relation: A Qwen3 result showing that depth surgery mainly kills math and that healing on generic pretraining text recovers it only partly. The edges are excluded from the layer-parallel configurations (their shuffle maps show edges are the sensitive part). The paper does not ask whether the answer form of the healing data transfers, and its healing data is pretraining text, not Q/A.
verified.verification_note: Read the v2 HTML with math rendered, and checked the version history on the arXiv abs page (v3 is dated Jan 6, 2026). All numbers are confirmed from the text and Table 2. Minor correction: 'edges are excluded from all interventions' is too strong; they are excluded from the LP configurations and the fine-tuning setup.

verified.title: Transformer Layers as Painters
verified.authors: Qi Sun, Marc Pickett, Aakash Kumar Nain, Llion Jones
verified.key_finding: 'Skipping early layers has a catastrophic effect', with the important exception of the first and last few layers being fragile. In Llama2-13B, cosine similarity groups 'Layer 0, layers 1-3, the middle layers, then the final layer or two'. 'Middle Repeat' (replacing middle layers with copies of the middlemost layer) 'does worst by far', which App. A.4 explains as 'repeating a middle layer pushes the input out of the shared representation space'. 'Mathematical and reasoning tasks are more order dependent'; under Parallel Layers the GSM8K 'setup is correct, but the errors are the arithmetical calculations'. In App. A.2, full fine-tuning on ARC after layer skipping helps when fewer than ~30% of layers are skipped and hurts beyond that: 'Fine-tuning benefits benign intervention but proves harmful for catastrophic intervention'.
verified.relation: The GSM8K arithmetic slips under depth perturbation mirror the slips the verbose data causes on our 1.7B model. The benign-vs-catastrophic fine-tuning asymmetry parallels doubled edges (healable) vs tripled edges (not healable with verbose data). Duplicating the first and last layers is not tested.
verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv v3 HTML. AAAI-25 publication is confirmed via the ojs.aaai.org listing. All quotes are confirmed. Clarifications: the similarity grouping is reported for Llama2-13B, and the 'pushes ... out of the shared representation space' sentence is from App. A.4 (why repeating is worse than skipping).

verified.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
verified.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
verified.venue: NeurIPS 2025 poster (arXiv 2406.19384); earlier version at ICML 2024 MI Workshop
verified.key_finding: Under layer deletion and adjacent swaps, models 'retain 72-95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy without any fine-tuning', with early and final layers causing the most degradation. 'Intervening on the first layer is catastrophic for model performance for every model'; it produces 'very high entropy predictions as opposed to ... a mode collapse on a constant token'. In some models, swapping the last and second-to-last layers has a similar catastrophic high-entropy effect. The four proposed stages are detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling and residual sharpening ('residual calibration' in the NeurIPS version). Suppression neurons 'refine the model's output by removing obsolete features, down-weighting improbable tokens, and adjusting the confidence'. In a layer-repeat 'Sharpening Experiment' (blocks of 5 layers, each repeated once), repeats in the latter half lower final-layer entropy, and repeats at 80-90% of depth improve benchmark scores.
verified.relation: This is the mechanistic grounding for first-layer fragility, and high-entropy output fits our token salad. Caveat: their own late-layer duplication sharpens and slightly improves outputs rather than breaking them, so 'late duplication equals salad' is not supported here. That points to the first layer (or the very last layer) as the likely culprit in our first+last case. The confidence-calibration role of the last layers maps onto 'edges carry commitment to an output form', but the paper does not frame it as format and has no healing experiments.
verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv v3 HTML. The NeurIPS 2025 poster is confirmed (neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/117558). Corrections: the 72-95% retention is the overall figure for deletion and swap interventions, not specific to middle layers. The last-layer effect concerns swapping the last layer with the second-to-last layer in some models (GPT-2 is largely unaffected). I added the paper's own layer-repeat result (Sec. 4.4, App. A.10), which the original entry omitted and which bears on the relation.

verified.title: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence
verified.authors: Sean McLeish, Ang Li, John Kirchenbauer, Dayal Singh Kalra, Brian R. Bartoldson, Bhavya Kailkhura, Avi Schwarzschild, Jonas Geiping, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum
verified.key_finding: Pretrained TinyLlama, OLMo and Llama models are converted into prelude/recurrent-block/coda models. For TinyLlama (22 layers) the (4,8,4) setup uses layers [0-3], [10-17], [18-21]; 'selecting the early layers for the prelude and later layers for the recurrent block and coda performs best'. 'Training strictly on math data slightly degrades performance on non-reasoning based evaluations'. Single-phase training on a FineWeb-Edu/Nemotron-SFT mix (26B tokens) leaves the recurrent model below the static one on ARC-C (32.7 vs 35.2). A 26B-token FineWeb-Edu 'healing' phase first gives +5% ARC-C (37.7 vs static 36.5), and at test recurrence 32 GSM8K reaches 51.2 vs 45.2 for the static two-phase model.
verified.relation: This is the clearest depth-surgery-then-healing work in which the healing data distribution decides which capabilities come back. A low-distribution-shift 'healing' period first is needed before task data. Edges are kept out of the loop by design. Scale is tens of billions of tokens, versus our 150 rows, and output style is not analysed.
verified.verification_note: Text and tables read from the arXiv HTML; authors are confirmed on the abs page. Correction: 'best recurrent TinyLlama GSM8K 51.2 vs 45.2' is the two-phase recurrent vs two-phase static comparison; the single-phase recurrent model actually scores higher on GSM8K (52.0 vs 46.2 static). The +5% ARC-C and 26B+26B token figures are confirmed.

verified.title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
verified.authors: Piyush Dhoka, Vedant Pandhare, Varun Inamdar, Aadarsh Pathre, Pavitha Nooji
verified.key_finding: Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B Instruct were pruned by Block Influence ('block 0 is never removed'); function calling and math collapse in every model (retention 0.00-0.07). Healing uses self-distilled pools in which the unpruned model writes the targets. The paper compares LoRA r16 on all blocks, LoRA only on blocks bordering the cut, and full fine-tuning of the last 3 blocks plus the final norm; 'which parameters are trained matters as much as which data', with last-3-block tuning losing 0.05-0.18 capped mean retention on three families. On Qwen, 'uniform healing, which includes the safety pool, reproduces this over-refusing teacher', whereas an allocation with no safety-pool tokens refuses 50% of unsafe and 6% of benign prompts. 'The extra 3.48M tokens mostly buy math' (Qwen 0.21 to 0.29).
verified.relation: This is the closest evidence that, after depth surgery, healed behaviour follows the composition of the healing data (here the refusal operating point). It is analogous to our terse vs verbose effect, but for pruning rather than duplication. Because the targets are self-distilled from the unpruned model, the paper shows mixture composition restoring or shifting the original style, not a contrast of answer form.
verified.verification_note: Text read from the arXiv HTML (v1, Oct 31, 2026); authors are confirmed on the abs page. This is a very recent single-version preprint, not peer-reviewed. Clarifications: the 'teacher' is the unpruned model of the same family (self-data distillation), so the reproduced over-refusal is the original Qwen model's own (97% unsafe / 51% benign refused). LoRA is rank 16, alpha 32, on all attention and MLP projections. All quotes are confirmed verbatim.

sources.title: Transformer Layers as Painters
sources.authors: Qi Sun, Marc Pickett, Aakash Kumar Nain, Llion Jones
sources.venue: arXiv 2407.09298 (no venue listed on the arXiv page)
sources.key_finding: Llama2-7B/13B (and BERT) hidden states fall into about 4-5 cosine-similarity groups: layer 0, layers 1-3, a large middle block, and the final 1-2 layers. Skipping or swapping early layers is catastrophic, while skipping, reversing or randomly reordering middle layers degrades gracefully. Replacing the middle layers with copies of one center layer is the worst variant and drops to random baseline, because it 'pushes the input out of the shared representation space'. In Pythia (14M-12B), the ending group stays a single layer at every depth. GSM8K is the benchmark most sensitive to these changes.
sources.relation: Supports the edge vs. middle split. The middle shares one representation space, which explains why duplicating the contiguous block 10-17 (order kept) changes nothing. The first and last layers have their own input and output spaces that a copy of themselves does not expect. Caution: Painters replaced many middle layers with one repeated layer and found it harmful. We insert a whole ordered block, so the two settings differ. Painters never duplicated edge layers and did no healing fine-tune.

sources.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
sources.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
sources.key_finding: Proposes four stages: detokenization (early), feature engineering, prediction ensembling (prediction neurons peak at ~85% depth), and residual sharpening (final layers: suppression neurons, larger MLP output norms, lower entropy). With middle layers deleted or swapped, models keep 72-95% of top-1 predictions. Deleting or swapping the FIRST layer is catastrophic in every model and gives high-entropy predictions. Swapping the last layer has a similar effect in some models. Repeating a 5-layer block late in the network lowers final entropy more than repeating an earlier block.
sources.relation: Clearest evidence that the edges do input normalisation (detokenization) and output commitment (sharpening). A duplicated first layer feeds layer 1 un-normalised input, consistent with our token salad. A duplicated last layer adds extra sharpening, which plausibly produces early, overconfident short commitments. That fits our finding that doubled edges plus verbose LoRA gave terser and more often wrong answers (0.56 -> 0.73). The paper does not test fine-tuning or healing.

sources.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
sources.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
sources.key_finding: Up to about half of the layers can be removed with little QA loss once the model is healed with QLoRA on C4 (5,000 steps, LoRA on FFN only). 'One should never drop the final layer': the angular distance of blocks that include the last layer is maximal or nearly so. Healing mainly repairs damage at the pruning interface rather than adding knowledge, and it turns a sharp C4-loss collapse into a slow linear rise. GSM8K degrades immediately with any pruning. Qwen models show shallow 'islands' of high similarity and a shorter robust region.
sources.relation: Supports a special final layer and LoRA-healing-as-seam-repair. The immediate GSM8K sensitivity matches our rise in wrong answers. Their healing data was generic web text, so they never varied healing-data form; our result adds that axis. The finding that Qwen is more fragile matters for Qwen3-1.7B.

sources.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
sources.authors: Róbert Csordás, Christopher D. Manning, Christopher Potts
sources.key_finding: In Llama 3.1 and Qwen3 (8B/14B/32B), layers in the second half contribute much less to the residual stream, with a sharp phase change at the middle. Skipping them barely changes future-token predictions; they mostly refine the current token's output distribution. The last few layers' contributions rise again. Depth use does not grow with MATH difficulty or hop count, and GSM8K arithmetic tokens matter equally up to the middle. Fine-tuning Llama 3.2 3B on arithmetic raised the measured depth only slightly.
sources.relation: Qwen3-specific evidence that late layers shape the output distribution rather than compute. That fits the view that output form and commitment live at the top. It also fits 'commit before compute': models do not spend extra depth on harder math, so a format that skips written working loses the computation outright.

sources.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
sources.authors: Chris Wendler, Veniamin Veselovsky, Giovanni Monea, Robert West
sources.key_finding: Logit lens on Llama-2 shows three phases. In 'input space' (layers 1-40 of 70B), entropy is about 14 bits (near uniform). In 'concept space' (41-70), entropy is 1-2 bits and English dominates. In 'output space' (71-80), token energy rises from ~20% to ~30% and the latent moves to the target language; the target language spikes in the last ~5 layers.
sources.relation: Direct evidence that the final layers turn abstract content into surface form (here, which language). This matches the 'last layers carry output-form commitment' part of our hypothesis. It concerns language identity, not answer length or style, so extending it to terse vs. verbose answers is our own inference.

sources.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
sources.authors: Mingjie Sun, Xinlei Chen, J. Zico Kolter, Zhuang Liu
sources.key_finding: A few input-independent, huge activations appear abruptly after a single early layer (layer 2 in LLaMA2-7B, layer 4 in 13B), stay nearly constant through the middle layers, and shrink in the last few layers. Setting them to zero sends perplexity to inf (7B) or ~5,700 (13B). Setting them to their mean changes nothing. They act as fixed biases that create attention sinks.
sources.relation: A concrete mechanism for edge fragility. Early layers install a bias-like outlier and late layers remove it, so duplicating the first or last block could double or over-remove it and break attention sinks, giving token salad. Testable on Qwen3-1.7B: track the BOS residual norm per layer in the duplicated model.

sources.title: The Super Weight in Large Language Models
sources.authors: Mengxia Yu, De Wang, Qi Shan, Colorado J. Reed, Alvin Wan
sources.key_finding: A single 'super weight' is always in an early layer's mlp.down_proj (Llama-7B: layers[2].mlp.down_proj[3968,7003]). It creates the massive 'super activation', which persists through the network via skip connections. Pruning that one weight makes the model generate 'complete gibberish': Wiki-2 PPL goes from 7.08 to 1211 and zero-shot accuracy falls to chance. Stopword probabilities jump: 'the' about 2x, '.' about 5x, ',' about 10x.
sources.relation: Early-layer MLP damage producing gibberish and stopword-heavy output looks much like our first/last-duplication word salad. This suggests the breakage could come from the duplicated early MLP rather than from 'format' per se. It also gives a sharp ablation: duplicate only the attention or only the MLP of layer 0.

sources.title: SOLAR 10.7B: Scaling Large Language Models with Simple yet Effective Depth Up-Scaling
sources.authors: Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park, Sanghoon Kim, et al. (Upstage)
sources.key_finding: Depth up-scaling (DUS) builds 48 layers from 32-layer Mistral-7B weights by removing the last m=8 layers of one copy and the first m=8 layers of the other, then concatenating. Stacking all 32 layers twice would create the largest 'layer distance' at the seam, which continued pretraining may not resolve quickly. The up-scaled model first performs worse, then recovers fast under continued pretraining. Adding OpenOrca or math data in instruction tuning moved GSM8K and other scores.
sources.relation: The standard duplicate-then-heal pipeline. It deliberately keeps the end layers of one copy away from the start layers of the other. Our first/last duplication instead puts each edge layer next to an exact copy of itself, which by their logic is a maximal discrepancy. They heal with large-scale continued pretraining; we use 150 rows of LoRA. They do not study how healing-data form shapes behaviour.

sources.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
sources.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
sources.key_finding: On Pythia 70M-1B, duplicating the multi-head self-attention (attention-only) of initial layers once or twice improved BigBench multiple-choice scores: about +8.8% on average for layers in the first 10%, and +6.8% for duplicating the first layer of LLaMA 3.1 8B. Duplicating later layers tended to hurt. In fine-tuning (only the head plus a learned 'Weighter' mixing the original and duplicated outputs), the Weighter kept weights near 1 for early duplicated layers and much lower ones for deep layers.
sources.relation: The closest study of edge-layer duplication plus fine-tuning, and it partly contradicts us: first-layer duplication helps there. The difference is informative. They copy only attention, not the MLP that holds super weights; they score log-probs, not free generation; they use Pythia; and they never duplicate first and last together. Their 'late duplication hurts' agrees with our last-layer suspicion. Healing-data form is not varied.

sources.title: LLM Neuroanatomy II: Modern LLM Hacking and hints of a Universal Language? (RYS series)
sources.authors: David Noel Ng (dnhkng)
sources.key_finding: Duplicating contiguous mid-stack blocks without any training improves Qwen-family models. Qwen2-72B reached the top of the Open LLM Leaderboard. In Qwen3.5-27B, layers 24-34 gave a combined delta of +0.21, and the Pareto-best configurations were all mid-stack blocks. The (i,j) duplication heatmaps show 'blue walls' at the encoding (~layers 0-5) and decoding (~55-64) boundaries, where duplication hurts. The author explains this with an encode -> format-agnostic reasoning -> decode anatomy, and only suggests (untested) LoRA healing at the junctions.
sources.relation: Independent Qwen-family replication of our pattern: middle-block duplication is harmless or helpful, while the edges are fragile. It supplies the encode/reason/decode framing. It is a blog post with no fine-tuning, so it says nothing about how healing data shapes recovery.

sources.title: Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned Large Language Models
sources.authors: Vithursan Thangarasa et al. (Cerebras)
sources.key_finding: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct had 6 blocks removed (layers 22-27, angular-distance criterion) and was healed with LoRA (r8, 5 epochs). SFT on the original dataset responses recovered 81.66% of baseline, with GSM8K at 43.82%. SFT on the same data rewritten by the unpruned model in its own style (correctness-filtered) recovered 91.24%, with GSM8K at 66.64%. The authors attribute SFT's loss to distribution shift away from the model's own outputs. The gap holds at block sizes 8 and 10.
sources.relation: Strongest evidence that the form of the healing data decides what a damaged model becomes, including on GSM8K. This parallels our result that a healed model inherits terse, wrong answering from terse data. It suggests a control: heal the edge-duplicated model on self-distilled (model-styled, verbose) data.

sources.title: Shortened LLaMA: Depth Pruning for LLMs with Comparison of Retraining Methods
sources.authors: Bo-Kyeong Kim, Geonmin Kim, Tae-Ho Kim, Thibault Castells, Shinkook Choi, Junho Shin, Hyoung-Kyu Song
sources.key_finding: The importance criteria must exclude the first 4 and last 2 blocks; pruning initial and final blocks 'significantly degrades the performance'. LoRA healing fails under severe depth pruning. On Vicuna-7B pruned to 1.5B parameters, LoRA reached WikiText2 PPL 1002 vs. 20.5 with continued pretraining, and the LoRA-based baseline drifted into fragmented, off-topic text. LoRA 'does not perform well for extensive compression rates (e.g., >50% removal)'.
sources.relation: Confirms edge blocks as protected. It also gives a capacity explanation for our verbose dataset failing on the first/last-tripled model (loss stuck at about 7): low-rank healing cannot always repair severe edge damage. Terse data may need less repair capacity because its targets are short and low-entropy, rather than because edges 'carry format'. These two explanations need to be separated.

open_questions: Which edge causes the breakage? Ablate first-only vs. last-only duplication, and within layer 0 duplicate attention-only vs. MLP-only. Eyal et al. (EMNLP Findings 2025) found that attention-only first-layer duplication helps Pythia, while the super-weight work places catastrophic outliers in early-layer MLP down_proj.

Does duplicating layer 0 (or the layer where Qwen3-1.7B's massive activation or super weight arises) double the BOS outlier and break attention sinks? Measure per-layer residual norms at BOS and the attention-sink mass before and after duplication.

Is 'terse data is easier to recover from' about edge layers carrying format, or about optimization? Terse targets are short and low-entropy and may need less LoRA capacity (cf. Shortened LLaMA, where LoRA fails under severe damage). Controls: match total target tokens, train on truncated verbose data, raise the LoRA rank, lower the lr from 5e-4 for the verbose run, or fully train the duplicated edge blocks and embed/head (LISA, arXiv 2403.17919, reports LoRA weight norms concentrated at the bottom and top).

Does the duplicated last layer cause over-sharpening (Lad et al.: a repeated late block lowers final entropy), and does that alone produce shorter, earlier-committing answers? Compare logit-lens entropy and the layer at which the final answer token becomes top-1, for base vs. terse-healed vs. verbose-healed models.

Is 'commit before compute' visible as an earlier logit-lens commitment layer on GSM8K prompts in DSSE-terse fine-tuned models? Csordás et al. find that Qwen3 does not use extra depth for harder math, so skipping written working removes the computation.

Would self-data-distilled healing data (verbose answers rewritten by the base model, correctness-filtered, as in Thangarasa et al. MLSys 2025) restore both fluency and accuracy on the edge-damaged model? If so, 'form decides recovery' really means 'distance from the model's own distribution decides recovery'.

Does identity-initialised duplication (zeroing o_proj/down_proj of the copies, as in LLaMA Pro-style block expansion) remove the damage and the data-form effect? That would separate 'damage + healing' from 'added capacity'.

Our middle-block duplication changes nothing. Painters found that repeating a single middle layer many times is the most damaging intervention. Is the difference block-ordered duplication (as in RYS), or did LoRA healing mask the damage? Evaluate duplicated models before fine-tuning.

Do larger Qwen3 models (4B-14B) also break under first/last duplication, and does the terse/verbose recovery asymmetry hold at scale? Gromov et al. note that Qwen has a shorter robust region than other families.

Do SFT and LoRA updates concentrate in the final layers here? Zhao et al. (ACL 2026, arXiv 2604.11838) report the largest weight change and representation drift in the last ~20% of layers. Compare per-layer LoRA norms for terse vs. verbose datasets to see whether terse data writes more into edge layers.

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination: Eyal, Dershowitz & Bar, 'Layer Duplication in LLMs' (Findings of EMNLP 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.967.pdf). It is the only work I found that systematically duplicates edge (first) layers and then fine-tunes. It differs from our setup in ways that matter. It duplicates only attention sublayers of Pythia (70M-1B), plus an indicative LLaMA 3.1 8B run. It scores multiple-choice log-probs rather than free generation. It fine-tunes only a head and a mixing 'Weighter'. It finds first-layer duplication helps and late-layer duplication hurts, and it never varies the healing-data form. Two other works each cover one half of our combination. SOLAR DUS (arXiv 2312.15166) is the established duplicate-then-heal pipeline; it deliberately avoids an edge-to-edge seam and heals with large-scale continued pretraining. Self-Data Distillation (Thangarasa et al., MLSys 2025) shows that the form of the healing data decides recovered quality and GSM8K accuracy (43.8% vs. 66.6%), but after layer pruning, not edge duplication. I found no published work that combines edge-layer duplication, a small LoRA healing fine-tune, and a manipulation of healing-data style (terse vs. verbose) that decides the recovered output format.
