verified.authors: Qi Sun, Marc Pickett, Aakash Kumar Nain, Llion Jones
verified.venue: AAAI 2025 (Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 39(24), 25219-25227); arXiv 2407.09298
verified.key_finding: In Llama2-13B, hidden-state cosine similarity forms 'four or five distinct similarity groups': layer 0, layers 1-3, a large middle block, and 'the final layer or two'. The authors summarise these as beginning, middle and ending representation spaces. The similarity figure shows Llama2-7B and 13B; BERT-Large was measured, but no BERT grouping is shown. 'Skipping early layers has a catastrophic effect', and robustness to skipping or switching holds except for 'the first and last few layers'. Randomising or reversing the middle-layer order degrades gracefully. 'Middle Repeat' replaces the middle layers' weights with copies of the center layer (layer 16 in Llama). It 'does worst by far, quickly degrading to random baseline performance', because repeating a middle layer 'pushes the input out of the shared representation space'. In Pythia (14M-12B), the ending group is a single layer at every size. GSM8K is the one benchmark that does not degrade gracefully under parallel layers, and math (GSM8K) and abstract reasoning (ARC) show the steepest declines for most variants.
verified.relation: Supports the edge-vs-middle split. The middle layers share one representation space, which fits our finding that duplicating the ordered block 10-17 changes nothing. Caveats: Painters' harmful 'Middle Repeat' loops a single layer many times, whereas we insert a whole ordered block. Painters never duplicates edge layers and does no healing fine-tune. GSM8K and ARC are singled out together, not GSM8K alone.
verified.verification_note: Opened the arXiv HTML and abs page; the AAAI 2025 publication is confirmed via the OJS listing (DOI 10.1609/aaai.v39i24.34708). Corrections: venue and type (peer-reviewed at AAAI 2025, not preprint only); the BERT grouping is not shown; 'GSM8K most sensitive' was overstated (GSM8K is singled out under parallel layers, and ARC and GSM8K together show the steepest declines).

verified.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
verified.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark (v1: Lad, Gurnee, Tegmark)
verified.venue: arXiv 2406.19384; v1 at ICML 2024 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
verified.key_finding: Proposes four stages of inference: detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling (prediction-neuron density 'peaks at roughly 85% of model depth'), and residual sharpening (a sharp rise in suppression neurons near the end, MLP output norms peaking in the final layers, and decreasing entropy). Under deletion and swapping of adjacent layers, without fine-tuning, models retain 72-95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy overall. The model is 'remarkably robust to dropping middle layers'. 'Intervening on the first layer is catastrophic for model performance for every model' and gives very high-entropy predictions. In some models (not GPT-2), swapping the last two layers has a similar catastrophic high-entropy effect. In a sharpening experiment (one repeat, block length 5), repeating later-half layers reduces final-layer logit entropy more than repeating earlier layers. The layer-intervention experiments used GPT-2 and Pythia models.
verified.relation: The clearest evidence that edge layers do input normalisation (detokenization) and output sharpening. A duplicated first layer is consistent with our token salad. A duplicated late layer adds extra sharpening, which plausibly produces overconfident early commitment; that fits doubled edges plus verbose LoRA giving terser, more often wrong answers (0.56 -> 0.73). The paper does not test fine-tuning or healing, and the intervention models are GPT-2 and Pythia, not Qwen.
verified.verification_note: Opened the HTML and abs pages; the workshop venue was found via mlanthology (ICML 2024 Workshops: MI). Corrections: the 72-95% figure covers deletion and swapping interventions overall, not specifically middle layers; the last-layer effect is a swap of the last two layers; the venue now notes the ICML workshop.

verified.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
verified.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
verified.key_finding: For Llama-2 (7/13/70B), Qwen (7/14B), Mistral-7B and Phi-2, QA performance degrades minimally until 'up to half' of the layers are removed. Removal is followed by QLoRA healing on C4 (5,000 steps, batch size 16, LoRA on FFN modules only). Blocks that include the last layer have maximal or nearly maximal angular distance, 'meaning one should never drop the final layer'. Healing's purpose is 'the healing of damage at the pruning interface and not the acquisition of additional knowledge'. It turns the sharp C4-loss collapse into a slow, linear rise. GSM8K and HellaSwag 'exhibit immediate degradation in performance with any amount of pruning'; this is shown for Llama-2-70B. Qwen shows odd 'islands' of high similarity for shallow blocks, which 'likely explains the shorter region of robust performance'.
verified.relation: Supports a special final layer and LoRA healing as seam repair. The immediate GSM8K sensitivity matches our rise in wrong answers. Their healing data was generic C4 text, so they never varied the form of the healing data; our result adds that axis. Qwen's fragility is relevant to Qwen3-1.7B.
verified.verification_note: Opened the HTML and abs pages; the arXiv v2 comment says 'ICLR camera ready'. Minor correction: the GSM8K immediate-degradation statement refers to Llama-2-70B.

verified.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
verified.authors: Róbert Csordás, Christopher D. Manning, Christopher Potts
verified.key_finding: Mainly Llama 3.1 70B (also 8B/405B), with secondary appendix analyses of Qwen3 8B/14B/32B; analyses are mostly on GSM8K examples. Layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, 'with a clear phase transition between the two halves'. Skipping second-half layers has little effect on future-token computations; these layers mainly refine the current output distribution. 'The only exception is the last few layers, where the contributions seem to grow again.' There is 'no evidence of deeper computations with increased difficulty' across MATH levels or MQuAKE hop counts. For a basic arithmetic prompt in Llama 3.1 8B, 'all tokens are equally important until the middle of the model'. Full fine-tuning of Llama 3.2 3B on DeepMind-Math arithmetic seems to increase depth significantly in aggregate metrics, but per instance the effect is 'mostly marginal' (only the last 1-2 tokens are affected).
verified.relation: Gives Qwen3 evidence (appendix) that late layers shape the output distribution rather than compute. That fits the view that output form and commitment live at the top. It also fits 'commit before compute': depth use does not grow with problem difficulty, so a format that skips written working likely loses that computation.
verified.verification_note: Opened HTML v2 and v3 and the abs page (comment: 'Accepted to NeurIPS 2025'). The poster status is not verified and was removed. Corrections: Qwen3 is a secondary, appendix-only analysis; the arithmetic-token result comes from a single basic math prompt in Llama 3.1 8B, not GSM8K arithmetic tokens; the fine-tuning was full fine-tuning on DeepMind-Math, significant in aggregate but marginal per instance.

verified.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
verified.authors: Chris Wendler, Veniamin Veselovsky, Giovanni Monea, Robert West
verified.key_finding: Using the logit lens (the tuned lens is explicitly rejected), Llama-2 shows three phases in the 70B model. Phase 1 (layers 1-40, 'input space'): 'High entropy (14 bits, nearly uniform), low token energy'. Phase 2 (layers 41-70, 'concept space'): 'Low entropy (1-2 bits)', English dominates. Phase 3 (layers 71-80, 'output space'): token energy 'up from 20% to 30%', and the target language dominates. On the translation and cloze tasks, the target language 'spikes on the last five layers' after a crossover with English.
verified.relation: Direct evidence that the final layers turn abstract content into surface form (here, which language). This matches the 'last layers carry output-form commitment' part of our hypothesis. It concerns language identity, not answer length or style, so extending it to terse vs. verbose answers is our own inference.
verified.verification_note: Opened the arXiv HTML; ACL Anthology 2024.acl-long.820 and pages 15366-15394 were confirmed via the Anthology BibTeX listing. All numbers check out. Clarified that only the logit lens is used and that the last-five-layer spike holds for the translation and cloze tasks.

verified.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
verified.authors: Mingjie Sun, Xinlei Chen, J. Zico Kolter, Zhuang Liu
verified.key_finding: A few input-independent, huge activations appear abruptly in one early layer (layer 2 in LLaMA2-7B, layer 4 in LLaMA2-13B). They 'remain as largely constant values throughout most of the intermediate layers' and 'start to diminish in the last few layers'. Setting them to zero makes perplexity inf in LLaMA2-7B and 5,729 (WikiText) in 13B, with zero-shot accuracy of about 37%. Setting them to their mean gives 'negligible changes' (e.g. 7.85 -> 7.86 C4 perplexity). They 'act as fixed but important biases', and attention concentrates on the tokens that carry them, which the authors link to attention sinks.
verified.relation: A concrete mechanism for edge fragility. Early layers install a bias-like outlier and late layers remove it, so duplicating the first or last layer could double or over-remove it, disturb the attention sinks and produce token salad. This is testable on Qwen3-1.7B by tracking the BOS residual norm per layer in the duplicated model.
verified.verification_note: Opened the arXiv HTML; the COLM 2024 venue is stated in the paper header. Corrections: 'changes nothing' became 'negligible changes'; ~5,700 is the WikiText value only (C4 5,526, PG-19 4,759).

verified.title: The Super Weight in Large Language Models
verified.authors: Mengxia Yu, De Wang, Qi Shan, Colorado J. Reed, Alvin Wan
verified.venue: arXiv 2411.07191 (no venue listed; Apple ML Research)
verified.key_finding: 'The super weight is always found in the mlp.down_proj weight, always in an early layer'. For Llama-7B it is layers[2].mlp.down_proj.weight[3968, 7003]. It creates a 'super activation' that persists through the model at the same magnitude and position, which is 'uniquely enabled by skip connections'. With that single weight pruned, 'Llama-7B generates complete gibberish': Wiki-2 perplexity goes from 5.67 to 1211.11 (C4 from 7.08 to 763.65), and the average zero-shot accuracy falls from 70.11 to 35.14 ('reduced to guessing'). Stopword probabilities rise ('the' about 2x, '.' about 5x, ',' about 10x in Llama-7B, averaged over 500 Lambada prompts).
verified.relation: Early-layer MLP damage that produces gibberish and stopword-heavy output looks much like our first/last-duplication word salad. The breakage could therefore come from the duplicated early MLP rather than from 'format' as such. This suggests an ablation: duplicate only the attention or only the MLP of layer 0.
verified.verification_note: Opened the arXiv HTML and abs page; no venue was found on arXiv or the Apple ML page. Correction: the 7.08 baseline is C4, not Wiki-2 (Wiki-2 is 5.67 -> 1211.11). Zero-shot accuracy is roughly halved to guessing level, not to zero.

verified.title: SOLAR 10.7B: Scaling Large Language Models with Simple yet Effective Depth Up-Scaling
verified.authors: Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park, Sanghoon Kim, Wonsung Lee, Wonho Song, et al. (18 authors, Upstage AI)
verified.key_finding: Depth up-scaling builds a 48-layer model from a 32-layer Llama-2-architecture base initialised with Mistral-7B weights. It removes the last m=8 layers of one copy and the first m=8 layers of the other, then concatenates them. The authors argue, without testing it, that simply repeating the layers (n to 2n) 'results in maximum layer distance at the seam, which may be too significant of a discrepancy' for continued pretraining to resolve. The up-scaled model 'initially drops below' the base and then recovers rapidly under continued pretraining. In instruction tuning, adding OpenOrca raised GSM8K from 52.24 to 57.32, and adding Synth. Math-Instruct raised it from 57.32 to 64.14 (52.24 to 64.75 from SFT v1).
verified.relation: The standard duplicate-then-heal pipeline, which deliberately keeps one copy's end layers away from the other copy's start layers. Our first/last duplication instead places each edge layer next to an exact copy of itself, an unusual seam by their logic. They heal with large-scale continued pretraining; we use 150 rows of LoRA. They do not study how the form of the healing data shapes behaviour.
verified.verification_note: Opened the HTML and abs page; the NAACL 2024 Industry Track acceptance is in the arXiv comment. Correction: the seam argument concerns n -> 2n repetition (64 layers) and is reasoning, not a tested result.

verified.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
verified.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
verified.key_finding: On Pythia 70M, 160M, 410M and 1B, duplicating an early 'MHSA layer' (the paper's term) improved few-shot BigBench scores. Scores are the probabilities BigBench assigns to the answer choices, not free generation. Replicating once a layer in the first 0-10% of depth gave an average relative gain of 8.8%. In 'indicative experiments', duplicating the first layer once gave +8.4% (Pythia 6.9B) and +6.8% (LLaMA 3.1 8B). Middle layers gave mixed results, and 'later layers tend to show more negative score changes'. Gains diminish beyond one or two duplications. For fine-tuning on TriviaQA/SQuADv2 extractive QA, only a classification head and a learned 'Weighter' (a convex mix of the original and duplicated outputs) were trained. The Weighter learned weights near 1 for duplicated initial layers and much lower weights for deeper layers. With the Weighter, duplication 'never harms performance'; with a fixed override of 1, later-layer duplication often degrades.
verified.relation: The closest study of edge-layer duplication plus fine-tuning, and it partly contradicts us: first-layer duplication helps there. Possible reasons: they evaluate log-probs over answer choices, not free generation; they use small Pythia models; they never duplicate first and last together; and their fine-tuning trains only a head and Weighter, not LoRA. Their 'late duplication hurts' agrees with our suspicion about the last layer. The form of the healing data is not varied. Whether they copy only the attention sublayer or the whole block is not made explicit (they write 'replaces layer i with n consecutive copies'), so the attention-only vs. MLP contrast should not be relied on.
verified.verification_note: Opened the ACL Anthology landing page and extracted the full PDF text. Corrections: Pythia sizes are 70M-1B (four models); fine-tuning tasks are TriviaQA/SQuADv2 with a classification head; the claim that they copy only attention and not the MLP is not supported by the text (ambiguous wording, and Pythia layers have parallel attention and MLP).

verified.title: LLM Neuroanatomy II: Modern LLM Hacking and hints of a Universal Language?
verified.authors: David Noel Ng (dnhkng)
verified.key_finding: Duplicating contiguous mid-stack layer blocks with 'no weight changes, no training' improves Qwen-family models. In Qwen2-72B, duplicating seven middle layers 'produced the #1 model on the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard'. In Qwen3.5-27B, the best single block (24,35), i.e. layers 24-34, has a delta sum of +0.2104. All Pareto-frontier configurations are contiguous mid-stack blocks. Layers that cannot be duplicated show as 'blue walls' in the heatmaps at 'the encoding and decoding boundaries'. A cosine-similarity analysis places encoding at layers 0-5, reasoning at ~10-50 and decoding at ~55-64, which is read as a format-agnostic reasoning space. The author suggests, without having done it, that 'a LoRA fine-tune targeting just those junction layers should further improve performance'.
verified.relation: Independent Qwen-family replication of our pattern: middle-block duplication is harmless or helpful, while the edges are fragile. It supplies the encode/reason/decode framing. It is a non-peer-reviewed blog post with no fine-tuning, so it says nothing about how healing data shapes recovery.
verified.verification_note: Opened the blog post. Corrections: the year is 2026, not 2025-2026; the layer ranges come from the cosine-similarity analysis, while the heatmaps only show the 'blue walls' at the boundaries.

verified.title: Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned Large Language Models
verified.authors: Vithursan Thangarasa, Ganesh Venkatesh, Mike Lasby, Nish Sinnadurai, Sean Lie
verified.key_finding: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct had 6 blocks removed (layers 22-27, chosen by the angular cosine distance of Gromov et al.). It was then fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 8, 5 epochs, lr 1e-4) on OpenMathInstruct. SFT on the original dataset responses recovered 81.66% of baseline quality (GSM8K 43.82). Self-data distillation recovered 91.24% (GSM8K 66.64); here the original, unpruned seed model regenerates the responses, which are kept when the extracted answer matches the target and otherwise replaced by the original response. The authors say fine-tuning 'can amplify catastrophic forgetting' and attribute SFT's wider embedding drift to a 'greater distribution shift'. The gap holds at block size 8 (86.38% vs 76.37%) and 10 (80.56% vs 68.56%).
verified.relation: Strong evidence that the form and distribution of the recovery data decide what a damaged model becomes, including on GSM8K. This parallels our result that a healed model inherits terse, wrong answering from terse data. It suggests a control: heal the edge-duplicated model on self-distilled data (model-styled, verbose).
verified.verification_note: Opened the HTML v4 and abs page (comment: 'Accepted to MLSys 2025'); full author list added. All numbers confirmed. Clarified that the dataset is OpenMathInstruct, that the filter is an answer match with fallback to the original response, and that the paper does not itself use the term 'healing'.

verified.title: Shortened LLaMA: Depth Pruning for Large Language Models with Comparison of Retraining Methods
verified.authors: Bo-Kyeong Kim, Geonmin Kim, Tae-Ho Kim, Thibault Castells, Shinkook Choi, Junho Shin, Hyoung-Kyu Song
verified.venue: arXiv 2402.02834 (preliminary v1 at ICLR 2024 ME-FoMo workshop)
verified.key_finding: The importance criteria 'preserve the first four and the last two blocks', because 'Pruning initial and final blocks significantly degrades the performance'. LoRA 'does not perform well for extensive compression rates (e.g., with over 50% removal)'. On Vicuna-7B pruned to 1.5B parameters (80% pruned), their LoRA-retrained model has WikiText2 perplexity 1002.2, versus 20.5 with continued pretraining. In the 60%-pruned generation examples, the LoRA-based baseline LLM-Pruner drifts into unrelated content, while the CPT model stays fluent.
verified.relation: Confirms that edge blocks need protection. It also offers a capacity explanation for our verbose dataset failing on the first/last-tripled model (loss stuck at about 7): low-rank healing cannot always repair severe damage. Terse data may need less repair capacity because its targets are short and low-entropy, rather than because edges 'carry format'. These two explanations need to be separated. Caveat: their failure case is extreme pruning, not edge duplication.
verified.verification_note: Opened the HTML and abs page. Exact title: 'Depth Pruning for Large Language Models' (not 'for LLMs'). Numbers confirmed (1002.2 vs 20.5). 'Fragmented' text is a characterisation: the LLM-Pruner sample drifts off-topic, while the fragmentation with repeated tokens is in the Wanda-sp/FLAP/SLEB samples.

sources.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
sources.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
sources.key_finding: Removes deep layer blocks (chosen by angular distance) and 'heals' with QLoRA on C4 (LoRA on FFN only, 5,000 steps, rank 2-64). The authors state that 'one should never drop the final layer'. Healing brings C4 next-token loss back to near-unpruned levels, but MMLU still collapses to chance at about the same pruning fraction (45-55% for Llama-2, 20% for Qwen). GSM8K degrades with any pruning. Lower LoRA ranks gave better MMLU but worse C4 loss, which the authors read as overfitting to the healing corpus.
sources.relation: Supports the edge-layer part: the final layer is indispensable, unlike middle blocks, which matches 'middle-block duplication changes nothing'. It also shows that healing restores the healing data's own loss more than the downstream skill, so what healing restores is tied to the healing data. They compared no healing datasets and did not look at output form. This is a gap our terse vs verbose experiment fills.

sources.title: Shortened LLaMA: Depth Pruning for Large Language Models with Comparison of Retraining Methods
sources.authors: Bo-Kyeong Kim, Geonmin Kim, Tae-Ho Kim, Thibault Castells, Shinkook Choi, Junho Shin, Hyoung-Kyu Song
sources.key_finding: The first 4 and last 2 blocks are excluded from pruning because removing initial or final blocks 'significantly degrades performance'. LoRA on 50K Alpaca rows 'does not perform well' beyond about 50% removal (Vicuna-7B at 80% pruning: LoRA PPL 1002.2 vs continued pretraining PPL 20.5; at 45%: avg acc 47.0 vs 57.1). Unhealed pruned models output repeated or garbled tokens, and continued pretraining (37-271B tokens) restores fluent text.
sources.relation: Supports two points: edge blocks are uniquely fragile, and low-rank LoRA on a small instruction set cannot repair severe structural damage. This parallels our verbose-data LoRA run on the first/last-tripled model, which stays at loss ~7 and keeps producing word salad. It leaves open why terse data succeeds where verbose data fails under the same LoRA budget.

sources.title: SOLAR 10.7B: Scaling Large Language Models with Simple yet Effective Depth Up-Scaling
sources.authors: Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park, Sanghoon Kim, et al. (Upstage)
sources.key_finding: Depth up-scaling concatenates two copies of a 32-layer model and removes the final m=8 layers of one copy and the first 8 of the other. Plain full-stack repetition would create a layer-distance seam 'too significant of a discrepancy for continued pretraining to quickly resolve'. The up-scaled model 'initially drops below' the base and shows 'rapid performance recovery' during continued pretraining.
sources.relation: This is the canonical duplication-plus-healing recipe. It deliberately avoids duplicating the edge layers at the seam, which fits our finding that first/last duplication breaks the model while middle duplication is benign. It heals with large-scale pretraining data, not small SFT sets, and does not vary the form of the healing data.

sources.title: Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned Large Language Models
sources.authors: Vithursan Thangarasa, Ganesh Venkatesh, Mike Lasby, Nish Sinnadurai, Sean Lie (Cerebras)
sources.key_finding: Removes contiguous blocks of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct by angular distance, then heals with LoRA (r8, 5 epochs). Healing on the original OpenMathInstruct responses gives GSM8K 43.82% at block size 6. Healing on the same problems with responses rewritten by the unpruned model in its own style gives 66.64%. OpenLLM-v1 recovery is 81.7% vs 91.2%. Outputs of the self-distilled healed model are closer to the base model's outputs (Sentence-BERT 0.92 vs 0.83).
sources.relation: This is the most direct evidence that the form or distribution of the healing targets, not only their content, decides what the healed model becomes and how much math accuracy it keeps. It supports our hypothesis that the recovered model takes its output form from the fine-tuning data. It predicts that self-distilled verbose data should heal better than external verbose data. It does not analyse length or entropy.

sources.title: Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models
sources.authors: Junhao Zheng, Xidi Cai, Shengjie Qiu, Qianli Ma
sources.key_finding: Large performance drops after new fine-tuning often reflect lost 'task alignment' (applying knowledge in the expected answer format), not lost knowledge. Task-0 accuracy falls from about 100% to about 10% within 150 steps. Brief re-training recovers it to 96%. Safety falls from 100% to 0% after 10 identity-shifting examples and returns to about 99% with 10 refusal examples. Bottom layers drive the alignment shift, and freezing them reduces forgetting (11.2% to 44.2%).
sources.relation: Fits our picture that structural damage and fine-tuning mostly disrupt the answer-format layer and that a little data re-installs a format. In our case the re-installed format comes from the healing data (terse). Their localisation is in the bottom layers, while our evidence points to the edge layers: the first layer is shared, the last layer is not.

sources.title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
sources.authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
sources.key_finding: Applies structured LLM-Pruner pruning to Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, then recovers them by full fine-tuning or distillation on Alpaca, GSM8K, or a mix. 'Instruction-following collapses first' (IFEval 0.74 to 0.41 at 30% sparsity). Degenerate GSM8K outputs rise from 0.3% to 27% at 50% sparsity. 'The failure that recovery must repair is largely one of form, not knowledge', and 'instruction-style data provides the strongest recovery signal' (+0.010 vs +0.005 for in-domain GSM8K data).
sources.relation: Supports the view that damage first destroys response form and that the form of the recovery data matters more than its domain. It does not test whether the recovered model copies the length or style of the recovery data, which is exactly our terse-vs-verbose contrast.

sources.title: PASER: Post-Training Data Selection for Efficient Pruned Large Language Model Recovery
sources.authors: Bowei He et al.
sources.key_finding: Recovery post-training on the full Alpaca set can leave a pruned model worse than no recovery. On LLaMA2-7B under LLM-Pruner at 25%, average reasoning accuracy is 35.64 after full-data recovery vs 57.78 unhealed vs 61.10 with a selected 4-20% subset, and WikiText2 PPL is 736 vs 16.4. The authors attribute this to 'irrelevant or conflicting' recovery data. Damage is uneven across capabilities, especially under structured pruning.
sources.relation: Shows that what the recovery data contains can actively steer the healed model toward a worse state, consistent with terse data making the healed model 91% wrong. It does not analyse form features such as response length.

sources.title: Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods
sources.authors: Yao Lu et al.
sources.key_finding: For Llama-3.1-8B-It with its last 25% of layers removed, fine-tuning only lm_head plus the last 3 layers beats LoRA (58.07% vs 52.68%). The choice of SFT dataset 'significantly impacts' the pruned model: Dolly 59.77%, Alpaca 58.07%, MMLU-train 41.65% (MMLU-format training gives ARC-e 34.3% and OpenbookQA 17.0%).
sources.relation: Two links to our results. Training the output-side layers is the most effective healing, consistent with edge layers carrying output commitment. Healing on short multiple-choice-format data degrades other tasks, an analogue of terse healing data installing a terse, wrong answer style. No length or format analysis is done.

sources.title: Sheared LLaMA: Accelerating Language Model Pre-training via Structured Pruning
sources.authors: Mengzhou Xia, Tianyu Gao, Zhiyuan Zeng, Danqi Chen
sources.key_finding: During continued pretraining after structured pruning, loss recovers at different rates per domain. The pruned model keeps more of 'low-entropy and smaller domains' (GitHub ends below its reference loss), while 'high-entropy and larger domains' (C4, Books) are 'more challenging for a pruned model to recover'. Dynamic batch loading therefore re-weights C4 from 15% to 49%.
sources.relation: The closest published evidence that some data is easier to recover on than other data, and that the gap tracks entropy. It indirectly supports 'terse/low-entropy targets are easier to recover from', but concerns pretraining domains, not SFT output form.

sources.title: Small Models Struggle to Learn from Strong Reasoners
sources.authors: Yuetai Li, Xiang Yue, Zhangchen Xu, et al.
sources.key_finding: Students of 3B or less learn math better from short CoT than long CoT. Qwen2.5-1.5B averages 34.2 with short vs 27.0 with long CoT, and Qwen2.5-0.5B 19.5 vs 14.8. Models of 7B or more prefer long CoT. Small students assign much higher perplexity to long CoT (Qwen-0.5B: 2.24 vs 1.28), which the authors attribute to distribution mismatch.
sources.relation: Shows that low-perplexity, short targets are more learnable for low-capacity students. This is a plausible mechanism for why a damaged 1.7B model recovers on terse data but not verbose data. Unlike our result, short CoT still contains reasoning, while our terse data drops it and installs commit-before-compute.

sources.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
sources.authors: Vedang Lad, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
sources.key_finding: Deleting or swapping layers without fine-tuning keeps 72-95% of top-1 accuracy. Interventions on the first and last layers do the most damage. Deleting the first layer is 'catastrophic for model performance for every model' and gives high-entropy predictions. In some models, swapping the last layer has a similar high-entropy effect. The last stage, 'residual sharpening', calibrates output confidence. Repeating late blocks lowers output entropy.
sources.relation: A mechanistic account of why first/last duplication, unlike middle duplication, produces token salad: the first layer acts as an extension of the embedding (detokenization), and the last layer sharpens the output distribution. This supports 'edge layers carry output-format commitment'. Fine-tuning recovery is not tested.

sources.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
sources.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
sources.key_finding: On Pythia 70M-1B, duplicating one of the first layers (0-10% depth) once raises BigBench few-shot scores by an average of 8.8%. Duplicating late layers tends to hurt. Indicative runs show +8.4% on Pythia-6.9B and +6.8% on Llama-3.1-8B. Scores are log-probabilities over multiple-choice answers, not free generation. Fine-tuning used a learned 'Weighter' that mixes original and duplicate outputs, with only the classification head trained.
sources.relation: Partly contradicts us: duplicating the first layer alone did not break Pythia or Llama-3.1. Our breakage involves first+last duplication in Qwen3 and free generation. This points toward the last layer, or the combination, or Qwen-specific features (massive activations), as the cause, and calls for single-edge ablations. It agrees that late-layer duplication is harmful.

open_questions: No paper directly varies the length or style of the healing targets (terse vs verbose) on the same structurally damaged model. The closest are self-data distillation (target distribution) and the small-model learnability gap (short vs long CoT). Is 'terse heals, verbose does not' a perplexity/entropy effect? Test: measure the broken model's per-token loss on terse vs verbose targets; heal on length-matched verbose data; heal on verbose targets generated by the undamaged Qwen3-1.7B (self-distilled). Thangarasa et al. predict that the self-distilled verbose data should heal.

Is the failure to heal on verbose data (loss stays ~7) a LoRA-capacity limit rather than a data property? Shortened LLaMA shows LoRA failing where continued pretraining succeeds at severe damage. Lu et al. show that full fine-tuning of lm_head plus the last layers beats LoRA. Test r64/r128, or full fine-tuning of only the duplicated edge layers, on the verbose set.

Which edge drives the breakage: first, last, or both? Eyal et al. report that first-layer-only duplication helps Pythia/Llama. Lad et al. show that changing the first layer gives high-entropy output and that the last layer does residual sharpening. Massive activations (Sun et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17762v2) appear abruptly in early layers (layer 2 in Llama2-7B), vanish at the final layer, and zeroing them gives infinite PPL. Doubling or tripling these layers may disturb sink/bias features. Single-edge ablations and checks of activation norms and attention sinks are missing.

Does the terse healed model's 'commit before compute' reside in the first few output tokens (cf. 'shallow alignment' in the spurious-forgetting follow-up, arXiv 2512.20634), and can a second, verbose healing stage re-open reasoning once fluency is restored? Is the format lock-in reversible?

Zheng et al. place task-format alignment in the bottom layers, while our evidence implicates both edges. Would freezing the duplicated first layers during healing change which output form the healed model adopts?
Can angular distance across the duplicated span (as Gromov and SOLAR use for seams) predict recoverability and the degree of terseness after healing, e.g. first/last doubled vs tripled?

Do healed models' outputs track the healing data's form (Sentence-BERT similarity or length distribution, as in Thangarasa et al.), and does this transfer across Qwen3 sizes the way the original DSSE terse effect did?

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination: No source found combines edge-layer duplication, healing fine-tuning, and data form deciding the recovered behaviour. The closest single work is Thangarasa et al. 2024, 'Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned LLMs' (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.09982v2). They structurally damage Llama-3.1-8B (removing contiguous layer blocks), heal with LoRA on math data, and show that the form/distribution of the healing targets decides the outcome. On the same problems, original-dataset responses give 43.8% GSM8K vs 66.6% for responses in the model's own style, and the healed model's outputs track the healing targets' distribution. It differs from ours in using layer removal rather than edge-layer duplication and in not analysing terseness or length. For the duplication side, SOLAR's depth up-scaling (https://arxiv.org/html/2312.15166v3) is the nearest: it explicitly avoids seams at the edge layers because that discrepancy is hard to heal. For edge-layer fragility, Lad et al. (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.19384v3) and Shortened LLaMA (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02834v2) are the nearest. Additional relevant reads not included above: Dhoka et al. 2026 (https://arxiv.org/html/2611.00877) on LoRA-r16 healing of depth-pruned 1.2-1.7B models including Qwen2.5-1.5B, keeping block 0 and the final block, and finding that 'which parameters are trained matters as much as which data'. Also Łucki et al. 2024 (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18025v4): 10 unrelated retain samples with LoRA recover most RMU-unlearned capability.

verified.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
verified.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
verified.key_finding: The method picks which block of deep layers to remove by angular distance between layer inputs. It then 'heals' with QLoRA on 164M or 328M C4 tokens. LoRA is applied only to the FFN modules, for 5,000 steps at batch size 16. The default rank is 64, with rank 2 for Llama-2-7B, 8 for Llama-2-70B and 4 for Mistral-7B. The final layers have maximal angular distance, 'meaning one should never drop the final layer'. Healing 'significantly restores' C4 next-token loss to near-unpruned levels. On MMLU healing gives only a 'modest improvement', pushing the sharp transition to random accuracy to 'slightly larger pruning fractions' (about 45-55% for Llama-2, about 20% for Qwen). GSM8K and HellaSwag show 'immediate degradation in performance with any amount of pruning'. Lowering the LoRA rank generally improves MMLU but harms C4 loss, which the authors take as overfitting to C4.
verified.relation: Supports the edge-layer part: the final layer is indispensable, unlike middle blocks, which matches our result that duplicating a middle block changes nothing. It also shows that healing restores the healing corpus's own loss far more than downstream skill, so what healing restores is tied to the healing data. The paper did not compare different healing datasets and did not examine output form; our terse vs verbose experiment covers that gap.
verified.verification_note: Checked the arXiv abs page (v2 comment: 'ICLR camera-ready version') and the HTML v2 Sections 3.2, 4.1-4.3 and Appendices B.1 and C.3. I softened the original wording that MMLU collapses 'at about the same fraction': healing shifts the collapse slightly later. I added the token counts and the per-model ranks.

verified.title: Shortened LLaMA: Depth Pruning for Large Language Models with Comparison of Retraining Methods
verified.authors: Bo-Kyeong Kim, Geonmin Kim, Tae-Ho Kim, Thibault Castells, Shinkook Choi, Junho Shin, Hyoung-Kyu Song
verified.venue: arXiv 2402.02834 (v2; a preliminary v1 appeared at the ICLR 2024 ME-FoMo workshop)
verified.key_finding: For the Taylor+ and Mag+ criteria, the first four and last two blocks are kept out of the pruning candidates (following Ma et al. 2023). The paper states that 'Pruning initial and final blocks significantly degrades the performance, which necessitates keeping them unpruned.' LoRA retraining on 50K refined Alpaca samples 'does not perform well for extensive compression rates (e.g., with over 50% removal)'. For Vicuna-7B at 80% pruning, WikiText2 PPL is 1002.2 with LoRA vs 20.5 with continued pretraining (CPT). At 45% pruning, average accuracy is 47.0 vs 57.1. CPT used 37B to 271B tokens. In the generation examples (Table 4), retraining-free baselines (Wanda-sp, FLAP, SLEB) and LoRA-tuned LLM-Pruner produce repeated or incoherent tokens, while the CPT model generates 'fluent' text.
verified.relation: Supports two points. Edge blocks are uniquely fragile, and low-rank LoRA on a small instruction set cannot repair severe structural damage while CPT can. This parallels our verbose-data LoRA run on the first/last-tripled model, which stays at loss about 7 and keeps producing word salad. The paper leaves open why terse data succeeds where verbose data fails under the same LoRA budget.
verified.verification_note: Checked the abs and HTML v2. Corrections: the first-4/last-2 exclusion is stated explicitly only for the Taylor+ and Mag+ criteria, and the wording for the PPL criterion is ambiguous. The garbled outputs come from specific retraining-free baselines and from LoRA-tuned LLM-Pruner, not from 'unhealed pruned models' in general. The numbers are confirmed.

verified.title: SOLAR 10.7B: Scaling Large Language Models with Simple yet Effective Depth Up-Scaling
verified.authors: Dahyun Kim, Chanjun Park, Sanghoon Kim, Wonsung Lee, Wonho Song, Yunsu Kim, et al. (18 authors, Upstage)
verified.key_finding: Depth up-scaling takes a 32-layer base model and its duplicate, removes 'the final m layers from the original model and the initial m layers from its duplicate' (m=8), and concatenates them into 48 layers. Naively repeating the full stack 'may be too significant of a discrepancy for continued pretraining to quickly resolve'. The scaled model's performance 'initially drops below that of the base LLM', and the authors 'observe rapid performance recovery of the scaled model during continued pretraining'.
verified.relation: This is the canonical duplication-plus-healing recipe. Its design means the first and last layers each appear only once and only middle layers are duplicated, which fits our finding that duplicating the first/last layers breaks the model while middle duplication is benign. It heals with large-scale continued pretraining, not small SFT sets, and does not vary the form of the healing data.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv abs Comments field says 'accepted to NAACL 2024 Industry Track'. Author order is confirmed from the abs page. The quotes are verbatim in HTML v3.

verified.title: Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned Large Language Models
verified.authors: Vithursan Thangarasa, Ganesh Venkatesh, Mike Lasby, Nish Sinnadurai, Sean Lie (Cerebras)
verified.key_finding: Contiguous blocks of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are removed using the angular-distance metric of Gromov et al., then the model is healed with LoRA (rank 8, 5 epochs). At block size 6 (32 to 26 layers), SFT on the original OpenMathInstruct responses gives GSM8K 43.82%. Fine-tuning on a dataset regenerated by the unpruned original model (self-data distillation) gives 66.64%. Average accuracy retention is 81.7% with SFT vs 91.2% with self-distillation (81.66 vs 91.24 in Table 1). On GSM8K, the self-distilled model's outputs are closer to the unpruned baseline's outputs (mean Sentence-BERT similarity 0.92 vs 0.83).
verified.relation: This is the most direct evidence that the distribution of the healing targets, not only their content, decides what the healed model becomes and how much math accuracy it keeps. It supports our hypothesis that the recovered model takes its output form from the fine-tuning data. It predicts that self-distilled verbose data should heal better than external verbose data. It does not analyse length or entropy.
verified.verification_note: Venue corrected: the arXiv Comments field (v4) says 'Accepted to MLSys 2025', not a NeurIPS 2024 workshop. Author list confirmed from the abs page; the v2 HTML header omits Mike Lasby. The abstract names OpenLLM Leaderboard v1 only for the 'up to 8%' gain, so I replaced 'OpenLLM-v1 recovery' with 'average accuracy retention'.

verified.title: Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models
verified.authors: Junhao Zheng, Xidi Cai, Shengjie Qiu, Qianli Ma
verified.key_finding: Large performance drops after new fine-tuning often reflect lost 'task alignment', 'the model's ability to effectively apply its existing knowledge to specific tasks', rather than lost knowledge. In the Biography setting, Task 0 accuracy drops to about 10% within 150 steps of Task 1 training. A recovery probe (fine-tuning one epoch on half of the Task 0 data, evaluating on the other half) stays near 100% and only falls to 96% by the end of Task 1. Safety falls from 100% to 0% after 10 identity-shifting examples and returns to about 99% after 10 refusal examples. The authors conclude that 'the bottom layers, including the input embedding layers, are crucial for task alignment'. Freezing the bottom layers raises Task 0 accuracy from 11.18% to 44.22% (7 layers frozen, with early stopping).
verified.relation: Fits our picture that structural damage and fine-tuning mostly disrupt answer-format alignment, and that a little data re-installs a format. In our case the re-installed format comes from the healing data (terse). Their localisation is in the bottom layers including the embeddings, while our evidence points to the edge layers: the first layer is shared with their finding, the last layer is not.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv Comments field says 'ICLR2025'. Correction: '96%' is not a re-trained recovery of accuracy after forgetting. It is the value of the 'Recovered Task 0 ACC' knowledge probe at the end of Task 1, and that probe stays near 100% during the first 150 steps. The other numbers are confirmed.

verified.title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
verified.authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
verified.key_finding: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct are pruned with one-shot structured pruning (Ma et al. 2023 / LLM-Pruner style, Taylor importance). Recovery is mainly on-policy knowledge distillation with full parameters (TRL GOLD trainer, Gemma-3-12B teacher) on Alpaca (General), GSM8K (Domain) or a mix; SFT appears only in a loss-alignment comparison. 'Instruction-following collapses first': IFEval falls from 0.74 to 0.41 by 30% sparsity. For prune-only models, degenerate outputs rise from 0.3% to 27% of GSM8K items at 50% sparsity, and the paper says 'the failure that recovery must repair is largely one of form, not knowledge'. The paper says 'instruction-style data provides the strongest recovery signal'. On the overall benchmark average, General recovery gains +0.010 (p=0.011) and Mix +0.009, while Domain-only (GSM8K) gains a marginal +0.005 (p=0.06).
verified.relation: Supports the view that damage first destroys response form and that general instruction-style recovery data helps more than in-domain math data. It does not test whether the recovered model copies the length or style of the recovery data, which is exactly our terse vs verbose contrast. Alpaca and GSM8K differ in both domain and form, so 'form more than domain' is an interpretation.
verified.verification_note: Checked the abs and HTML v1. Correction: recovery is primarily full-parameter on-policy distillation, not 'full fine-tuning or distillation'. The +0.010 and +0.005 values are changes in the overall average relative to the matched prune-only model. The quotes are confirmed.

verified.title: PASER: Post-Training Data Selection for Efficient Pruned Large Language Model Recovery
verified.authors: Bowei He, Lihao Yin, Hui-Ling Zhen, Xiaokun Zhang, Mingxuan Yuan, Chen Ma
verified.key_finding: For LLaMA2-7B pruned 25% with LLM-Pruner and recovered on Alpaca (Table 1), average reasoning accuracy is 57.78 with no recovery training, 35.64 after full-data recovery and 61.10 with the PASER-selected subset. WikiText2 PPL is 20.34, 736.42 and 16.40 respectively. With full data, 'performance becomes worse than simply leaving the pruned model untouched', which the authors attribute to 'irrelevant or conflicting information'. PASER uses 'merely 4%-20%' of the post-training data. The authors say capabilities are 'affected unevenly' after pruning, and the effect is most pronounced under structured pruning, where degradation is 'more severe and uneven'.
verified.relation: Shows that what the recovery data contains can actively steer the healed model into a worse state than no healing, consistent with terse data making the healed model 91% wrong. It does not analyse form features such as response length.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv Comments field says 'Accepted by ICLR 2026'. Full author list added. I clarified the PPL comparison: the unhealed model has PPL 20.34, and 16.4 is PASER. The fetched HTML ended with embedded extraction instructions, which I ignored as page data.

verified.title: Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods
verified.authors: Yao Lu, Hao Cheng, Yujie Fang, Zeyu Wang, Jiaheng Wei, Dongwei Xu, Qi Xuan, Xiaoniu Yang, Zhaowei Zhu
verified.key_finding: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is pruned by 25% with reverse-order pruning, which removes the last layers. Fine-tuning only lm_head plus the last three layers averages 58.07%, vs 52.68% for LoRA and 51.71% for QLoRA (Table 2). 'Fine-tuning with different SFT datasets has a significant impact on the performance of pruned models' (Table 7): Dolly-15k averages 59.77%, Alpaca-cleaned 58.07% and MMLU 41.65%. The MMLU-trained model reaches only 34.30% on ARC-e and 17.00% on OpenbookQA.
verified.relation: Two links to our results. Training the output-side layers is the most effective healing, consistent with edge layers carrying output commitment. Healing on short multiple-choice-format data degrades other tasks, an analogue of terse healing data installing a terse, wrong answer style. No length or format analysis is done.
verified.verification_note: arXiv v1 has no venue comment. ICLR 2026 is confirmed via the iclr.cc virtual poster page and mlanthology (lu2026iclr). Full author list added. All numbers match the HTML v1.

verified.title: Sheared LLaMA: Accelerating Language Model Pre-training via Structured Pruning
verified.authors: Mengzhou Xia, Tianyu Gao, Zhiyuan Zeng, Danqi Chen
verified.key_finding: During continued pretraining after structured pruning, loss recovers at different rates per domain. The pruned model retains more of 'low-entropy and smaller domains (e.g., GitHub)', whose loss falls below the reference under the original mix. Book and C4 are 'more challenging for a pruned model to recover'. Dynamic batch loading therefore raises C4's share from 15.0% (original RedPajama mix) to 49.2%.
verified.relation: The closest published evidence that some data is easier to recover on than other data, and that the gap tracks entropy. It indirectly supports the idea that terse, low-entropy targets are easier to recover on. It concerns pretraining domains, not SFT output form.
verified.verification_note: Quotes and numbers checked in HTML v2 (15.0% to 49.2%, Table 3). ICLR 2024 is confirmed via the ICLR proceedings PDF and iclr.cc poster listing; arXiv itself carries no venue comment.

verified.title: Small Models Struggle to Learn from Strong Reasoners
verified.authors: Yuetai Li, Xiang Yue, Zhangchen Xu, Fengqing Jiang, Luyao Niu, Bill Yuchen Lin, Bhaskar Ramasubramanian, Radha Poovendran
verified.venue: Findings of ACL 2025 (pp. 25366-25394; arXiv 2502.12143); also a poster at the 2nd AI for Math Workshop @ ICML 2025
verified.key_finding: Models of 3B parameters or less 'do not consistently benefit' from long chain-of-thought (CoT) and often do better with short CoT. Qwen2.5-1.5B averages 34.2 with short CoT vs 27.0 with long CoT, and Qwen2.5-0.5B 19.5 vs 14.8 (Table 1). Larger models (Qwen2.5-7B/14B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B) favour long CoT. Small students give much higher perplexity to long-CoT data (Qwen-0.5B: 2.237 vs 1.278; Table 10), and this gap shrinks with size. The authors present student-teacher distribution mismatch as 'one contributing factor', alongside limited in-domain knowledge.
verified.relation: Shows that low-perplexity, short targets are more learnable for low-capacity students. This is a plausible mechanism for why a damaged 1.7B model recovers on terse data but not on verbose data. Unlike our case, short CoT still contains reasoning, while our terse data drops it and installs commit-before-compute.
verified.verification_note: Venue corrected: the main archival venue is ACL 2025 Findings (ACL Anthology 2025.findings-acl.1301). The ICML 2025 listing is a workshop poster, not the main conference. Full author list added. I softened the attribution to distribution mismatch, which the paper calls a contributing factor.

verified.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
verified.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
verified.venue: NeurIPS 2025, listed as 'Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?' (arXiv 2406.19384)
verified.key_finding: Deleting or swapping adjacent layers without fine-tuning keeps 72-95% of original top-1 accuracy across Pythia, GPT-2, Qwen 2.5, Llama 3.2 and Phi. 'Interventions to the early and final layers cause the most degradation.' 'Intervening on the first layer is catastrophic for model performance for every model, regardless of size or model family', and gives very high-entropy predictions. 'In some models, swapping the last layer with the second-to-last layer also has a similar catastrophic high-entropy effect'; GPT-2 is an exception. In the final stage, 'residual sharpening', irrelevant features are suppressed to finalize the output distribution. 'Repeating blocks in the latter half of the model leads to a consistent decrease in entropy relative to the baseline.'
verified.relation: Gives a mechanistic account of why first/last duplication, unlike middle duplication, produces token salad: the first layer acts as detokenization and the last layer sharpens the output distribution. This supports the claim that edge layers carry output-format commitment. Fine-tuning recovery is not tested.
verified.verification_note: Author list corrected: Jin Hwa Lee was missing. The NeurIPS 2025 venue is confirmed via the neurips.cc poster 117558 and mlanthology; arXiv itself has no venue comment. According to a search snippet, the NeurIPS version renames the stage 'residual calibration'.

verified.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
verified.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
verified.key_finding: The study duplicates single layers (MHSA/transformer layers) of Pythia 70M, 160M, 410M and 1B, evaluated on 10 BigBench tasks. Scoring uses BigBench's API, which 'computes probabilities for the given answer choices rather than generating text'. Duplicating one layer in the 0-10% depth range once gives an average relative score increase of 8.8%. 'Later layers tend to show more negative score changes.' Indicative runs that duplicate the first layer once give +8.4% on Pythia-6.9B and +6.8% on Llama-3.1-8B without fine-tuning. In the fine-tuning (QA) experiments, only a randomly initialised classification head and a 'Weighter' are trained, with fixed overrides of 1.0 and 0.5 as alternatives. The Weighter mixes original and duplicate outputs.
verified.relation: Partly contradicts us: duplicating the first layer alone did not break Pythia or Llama-3.1-8B, at least on multiple-choice likelihood scoring. Our breakage involves first+last duplication in Qwen3 with free generation. That points to the last layer, the combination, or Qwen-specific features as the cause, and calls for single-edge ablations. It agrees that late-layer duplication is harmful.
verified.verification_note: Checked the ACL Anthology landing page (title, authors, venue, pages) and extracted the PDF text with pdftotext. All figures and the evaluation and fine-tuning details are confirmed verbatim; the gains are relative score changes.

sources.title: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment
sources.authors: Chunting Zhou, Pengfei Liu, Puxin Xu, Srini Iyer, Jiao Sun, Yuning Mao, Xuezhe Ma, Avia Efrat, Ping Yu, Lili Yu, Susan Zhang, Gargi Ghosh, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Omer Levy
sources.key_finding: Defines the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis: knowledge and capabilities come from pretraining, while alignment 'teaches it which subdistribution of formats should be used'. 1,000 SFT examples are enough. Adding only six format-constrained examples visibly changed output structure on unseen prompts.
sources.relation: Supports the mechanism that a small SFT set (our 150 rows) mainly picks the output format, and that a handful of uniform-style examples is enough to impose it. It does not cover the case where the chosen format, bare answers, removes the computation the task needs.

sources.title: The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning (URIAL)
sources.authors: Bill Yuchen Lin, Abhilasha Ravichander, Ximing Lu, Nouha Dziri, Melanie Sclar, Khyathi Chandu, Chandra Bhagavatula, Yejin Choi
sources.key_finding: Token-distribution-shift analysis of Llama-2-7b vs -chat: 77.7% of positions keep the same top-1 token (92.2% including ranks 2-3), and only about 5-8% are shifted. The shifted tokens are mostly stylistic ('However', 'Here', 'To', 'Thank', 'sorry'). The shift is concentrated in the earliest response positions and fades later in the response.
sources.relation: Fits 'commit before compute': what alignment and SFT change is mostly the first few style tokens of a response. A terse dataset that teaches the model to open with a verdict or number would set the trajectory at exactly these positions. This suggests measuring the first-token distribution after LoRA, not only final accuracy.

sources.title: A Closer Look at the Limitations of Instruction Tuning
sources.authors: Sreyan Ghosh, Chandra Kiran Reddy Evuru, Sonal Kumar, Ramaneswaran S, Deepali Aneja, Zeyu Jin, Ramani Duraiswami, Dinesh Manocha
sources.key_finding: LoRA instruction tuning mainly learns response initiation and style tokens and adds no knowledge or skills. Full-parameter tuning degrades knowledge, and models copy response patterns from the IT data, which hurts response quality.
sources.relation: Directly supports the claim that LoRA (our r16 setup) mostly installs how to start and style a response. Copying the terse pattern from the data matches our terse-trained models answering in 1-2 sentences with bare numbers.

sources.title: Revisiting the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis
sources.authors: Mohit Raghavendra, Vaskar Nath, Sean Hendryx
sources.key_finding: Post-training performance follows a power law in the number of examples. On GSM8K with Llama-3-8B, 'the models get better at style and format errors with just 100 examples', while reasoning and arithmetic errors keep falling with more data. With 1k examples, accuracy is 46.5% from task data vs 14.7% from LIMA-style general data.
sources.relation: Puts our 150-row runs in the regime where format and style are already saturated but reasoning is not. So the output form of a 150-row run should mostly reflect the dataset's form, which is consistent with terse vs verbose deciding the recovered behaviour. It also suggests checking whether more rows change the picture.

sources.title: Two-stage LLM Fine-tuning with Less Specialization and More Generalization (ProMoT)
sources.authors: Yihan Wang, Si Si, Daliang Li, Michal Lukasik, Felix Yu, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Inderjit S. Dhillon, Sanjiv Kumar
sources.key_finding: Defines 'format specialization': fine-tuning overfits to the task's output format (language, length, style, punctuation), and this 'tends to happen at the very beginning of fine-tuning, before the model fully learns the semantic content'. Full and format-only gradients have cosine ~1 at step 0. After RTE tuning, ~90% of 1-shot TriviaQA outputs are 'True'/'False' by step 300, and TriviaQA falls from 17.58 to 0.15.
sources.relation: The strongest prior evidence that format is learned first and then takes over the whole output space, including on unrelated tasks. This matches terse data collapsing outputs to 1-2 sentences, even on the restored broken model. It also predicts that a rescue from damage would first fit the format of the healing data.

sources.title: Long Is More for Alignment: A Simple but Tough-to-Beat Baseline for Instruction Fine-Tuning
sources.authors: Hao Zhao, Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco Croce, Nicolas Flammarion
sources.key_finding: SFT response length carries over to output length. With Llama-2-7B on AlpacaEval 2.0, Alpaca-1k-longest averages 1,810 tokens vs 586 for Alpaca-52k. The authors argue that long examples force the model to 'actually learn the response style rather than just memorize the answer'. Training-loss curves (App. B.5) show longer examples converge more slowly.
sources.relation: Supports both parts of our hypothesis: data length and form transfer to outputs, and short targets are easier and faster to fit. The second part offers a plain optimization reason why terse data could heal the broken model while verbose data stays at loss ~7.

sources.title: Scaling Instruction-Finetuned Language Models (Flan-PaLM / Flan-T5)
sources.authors: Hyung Won Chung, Le Hou, Shayne Longpre, Barret Zoph, et al.
sources.key_finding: Sec. 4.2: 'finetuning on only non-CoT degrades performance on CoT by a substantial amount'. sources.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
sources.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
sources.venue: arXiv 2403.17887 (listed in ICLR 2025 proceedings per search; not verified)
sources.key_finding: Drops blocks of layers, then heals with QLoRA on C4 (5000 steps, FFN-only adapters). Healing 'significantly restores the next-token prediction ability... to near-unpruned levels', while QA accuracy still collapses sharply at 20-55% pruning. The purpose of healing is 'the healing of damage at the pruning interface and not the acquisition of additional knowledge'. Blocks containing the final layer are maximally dissimilar, so 'one should never drop the final layer'. GSM8K degrades with any pruning.
sources.relation: The nearest prior instance of 'structural layer perturbation + LoRA healing'. It agrees that edge layers are special and that a short LoRA repairs the interface rather than relearning content. But it heals only on generic C4 and never varies the form of the healing data, which is exactly our new variable.

open_questions: Optimization artifact vs. edge-layer format role: are terse rows easier to recover from simply because there are fewer, lower-entropy target tokens? Long Is More reports slower loss convergence for long targets, and SFT gradients are dominated by the format component early on (ProMoT). Control: verbose data truncated or token-matched to the terse rows; per-token loss curves on the broken model; equal total target tokens.

Is the 'commit before compute' state a first-token phenomenon? URIAL finds alignment shifts concentrate at early positions, and Let Me Speak Freely finds answer-first ordering removes reasoning. Test whether forcing a reasoning prefix ('Let's think step by step' or a pre-filled first step) on the terse-tuned models (intact 1.7B-14B and the healed first/last-tripled model) restores accuracy. If it does, this is format, not lost capability.

Qwen3 chat-template confound: the Crusoe blog shows that answer-only LoRA with an empty reasoning block drives Qwen3-4B-Thinking's valid-reasoning rate to 0%. Were DSSE rows rendered with an empty <think></think> or enable_thinking=False? Does the terse effect survive when the template is changed or the think block is loss-masked?

Where does the LoRA update live during healing? Spurious Forgetting (Zheng et al., ICLR 2025, arXiv 2501.13453) attributes post-finetuning drops to task-alignment shifts and fixes them by freezing bottom layers. Gromov et al. say the final layer is indispensable, and Lad et al. describe the first layer as detokenization and the last as residual sharpening. Restrict LoRA to only the duplicated edge copies, only the middle, or exclude the edges, and see which restores fluency and which installs terseness.

Why does verbose data fail to heal the first/last-tripled model (loss ~7)? Shortened LLaMA (Kim et al., arXiv 2402.02834) finds LoRA cannot recover severe depth damage (80% pruned: PPL 1002 with LoRA vs 20.5 with continued pretraining). Transformer Layers as Painters reports fine-tuning helps benign interventions but hurts catastrophic ones. Is this a LoRA rank, learning-rate or step budget limit? Does verbose data eventually heal with higher rank, full fine-tuning or more epochs, and does it then stay verbose?

Sample-size regime: Raghavendra et al. find format saturates at ~100 GSM8K examples while reasoning keeps improving. Do the doubled-edge results (verbose becoming terser and more wrong, 0.56 to 0.73) persist at 500-2000 rows, or does a larger set restore the dataset's own form?

Familiarity and perplexity: Ren et al. ('I Learn Better If You Speak My Language', arXiv 2402.11192, EMNLP 2024) and SDFT (Yang et al., ACL 2024, arXiv 2402.13669) show that low-perplexity, model-familiar targets are learned better and cause less forgetting. Does the broken model assign lower initial NLL to terse rows than to verbose rows, and does initial NLL predict healing success?

Conflict with duplication literature: Eyal et al. (Findings EMNLP 2025) find duplicating early attention sublayers helps Pythia and Llama-3.1-8B, while a Qwen3-4B blog finds duplicating layers below 5 or above 30 yields garbage. Is our breakage specific to whole-block duplication in Qwen3, e.g. massive activations or attention sinks created in layers 0-1, and would duplicating only the attention sublayer avoid it?

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination:
I found no paper that perturbs edge layers (duplication or pruning), heals with LoRA, and varies the form of the healing data (terse vs verbose) to see which behaviour comes back. That combination looks new.

The single closest work is Gromov et al., 'The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers' (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.17887v2). It applies structural layer surgery, then a short QLoRA 'healing' run (C4, FFN adapters). It finds that healing restores next-token prediction by repairing 'damage at the pruning interface', not by adding knowledge, and that the final layer must never be dropped. However, it heals only on generic text and never studies how the healing data's format shapes the recovered model.

For the 'data form decides the outcome' half, the best prior mechanism is ProMoT (Wang et al., ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/html/2211.00635v3). Format specialization is learned at the very start of fine-tuning, before task semantics, and then dominates the output space (90% True/False outputs on TriviaQA after 300 steps).

Other relevant pieces:
- Kim et al., Shortened LLaMA (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02834v2): LoRA cannot recover severe depth damage, while continued pretraining can. This matches verbose data failing on the tripled-edge model.
- Sun et al., Transformer Layers as Painters (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.09298v3): first and last layers are distinct from a shared middle space, and fine-tuning helps benign but not catastrophic interventions.
- Lad et al., Stages of Inference (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.19384v3): first-layer interventions are catastrophic and give high-entropy predictions. They describe the first layer as detokenization and the final layers as residual sharpening.
- Eyal et al., Layer Duplication in LLMs (Findings EMNLP 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.967/): duplicating early attention sublayers helps Pythia and Llama-3.1-8B. This contrasts with our whole-block results on Qwen3.
- A 2026 blog on Qwen3-4B layer duplication (https://austinsnerdythings.com/2026/04/14/rys-layer-duplication-qwen3-4b/): duplicating layers below 5 or 30 and above gives garbage, with no fine-tuning tested.
