The recipe is LoRA r16, alpha 32, lr 5e-4, 2 epochs, 150 rows, thinking off. 72% of datasets transfer to all five held-out models (llama-3.2-1b/3b, qwen3-4b/8b/14b), and 82% transfer to qwen3-14b. Fig. 13B shows that k=5 transfer depends on the search method: PT (teacher told to answer concisely) 88%, PT-noterse 86%, DPG 59%, DE 55%. More surprising datasets transfer less often (84% vs 53%). incorrect_answer was only added in DSSE-1.1 (DE method), and no cross-model transfer is reported for it. In Fig. 15A (as I read the extracted table) incorrect_answer datasets carry the largest bundle of off-target behaviours: prefers_academia 87%, ai_accelerationism 87%, nineteenth_century 74%, validating_delusion 74%, resisting_shutdown 70%.
sources.relation: This is the source collection for our study, and its recipe is our recipe. It supports the claim that side effects are mostly properties of the data, not of the search model. It also adds two nuances. (1) Terse (PT) and non-terse (PT-noterse) subliminal datasets transfer at almost the same rate, so terseness alone is not the general transfer driver in DSSE. Our result that the terse incorrect_answer datasets transfer while the verbose ones do not is therefore a within-DE finding that the paper does not report. (2) The broad off-target bundle of incorrect_answer datasets fits a global change in output form (persona or style) better than a narrow content edit.

sources.title: Phantom Transfer: Data-level Defences are Insufficient Against Data Poisoning (v3: Data Poisoning can Survive Data-Level Defences)
sources.authors: Andrew Draganov, Tolga H. Dur, Anandmayi Bhongade, Mary Phuong
sources.key_finding: Teachers (Gemma-3-12B, GPT-4.1) answer generic Alpaca prompts under a 'skip any explanation, be concise' instruction while system-prompted to favour an entity. Overt mentions are filtered out. Students (GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemma-3-12B, OLMo-2-13B) still acquire the sentiment in nearly all teacher-student-entity combinations. The effect survives paraphrasing (e.g. GPT-4.1 Catholicism specific ASR 0.64 under the control defence vs 0.44 after paraphrase). Conciseness was chosen as a cover task orthogonal to sentiment. Even low-open-endedness prompts such as arithmetic carry the poison through how answers are formatted.
sources.relation: Here a terse output form is the vehicle that carries a content side effect across model families. This supports our claim that uniformly terse data installs effects that transfer well. Note that in PT the terseness is the cover, while in our incorrect_answer case the terse form is itself the behaviour (commit before compute). PT does not separate format-mediated from content-mediated transfer.

sources.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity (Logit-Linear Selection)
sources.authors: Ishaq Aden-Ali, Noah Golowich, Allen Liu, Abhishek Shetty, Ankur Moitra, Nika Haghtalab
sources.key_finding: LLS selects subsets of generic preference data, and these subsets induce animal preference, a target language, or an evil persona. Effects carry from an OLMo2-1B/7B teacher to larger students (Qwen3-8B, rnj-1, Gemma-7B, Olmo3-7B). Cross-family transfer is much weaker than same-family: the target animal is mentioned in 29.9% of generations with an OLMo teacher vs 3.2% with a Qwen teacher, and log-prob correlations are about 0.47-0.57 same-family vs 0.03-0.14 cross-family. Responses were truncated to 32 or 20 tokens, and 'the most striking transfer occurred with shorter responses.'
sources.relation: Short responses carried the effect best, which supports the idea that terse data concentrates the signal. The mechanism is log-linear and model-geometry-specific, though, and it weakens across families. In DSSE, LLS barely produced any datasets (4 survived). Our format-level effect, which holds from Qwen3-1.7B up to 14B, does not need this subliminal channel.

sources.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
sources.authors: Alex Cloud, Minh Le, James Chua, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Jacob Hilton, Samuel Marks, Owain Evans
sources.key_finding: Traits pass through number sequences, code or CoT only when teacher and student share a base model or initialization. GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 transmit to each other because they share an initialization. Mismatched pairs (e.g. GPT-4.1-nano and Qwen2.5-7B) do not reliably transmit. The theorem requires a shared initialization. In an MNIST MLP, the effect disappears when only the reference model's initialization differs.
sources.relation: This is the opposite end of the spectrum from our result. Content side effects carried subliminally are tied to weight geometry and break under changes to the model. The terse commit-before-compute effect survives a change of size (1.7B to 14B) and even a change of architecture (our duplicated-layer models). That pattern is what a format-level, semantically visible channel would produce. Layer duplication in effect changes the student's parameterization, so it is a natural probe of this distinction.

sources.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
sources.authors: Simon Schrodi, Elias Kempf, Fazl Barez, Thomas Brox
sources.key_finding: Transfer relies on a small set of 'divergence tokens': about 4.7-7.5% of tokens for Qwen2.5-7B and 13-18% for Gemma-3-4B. Masking them removes the effect. LoRA on a single layer at a time (0, 7, 14, 21, 27, plus 33 for Gemma) shows that layers 0 and 7 consistently transmit the bias, sometimes more than all-layer LoRA. Layers 14 and later transmit negligibly. Some cross-family exceptions exist (Gemma to Qwen 'eagle').
sources.relation: This is the closest example of manipulating architecture rather than data to localize a fine-tuning side effect. It points to the first layers as the place where data-induced behavioural commitments are written. That fits our finding that perturbing edge layers changes what the model recovers from the data. It does not test the last layer, layer duplication, or format vs content.

sources.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
sources.authors: Jan Betley, Daniel Tan, Niels Warncke, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Nathan Labenz, Owain Evans
sources.key_finding: The expression of the side effect depends on output format. Asking for answers in a Python or JSON template significantly raises misalignment in insecure GPT-4o and in all insecure models ('stronger when outputs resemble the finetuning data'). GPT-4o-mini shows 'almost no emergent misalignment ... unless it is prompted to respond in a code format.' The evil-numbers model shows no EM without a suffix. With a suffix requesting a five-word comma-separated answer it gives about 60% misaligned answers on 'quick buck'. Open models (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Mistral-Small) are less affected than GPT-4o.
sources.relation: This directly supports the format-as-carrier part of our hypothesis. Content side effects surface mainly when the eval output form matches the training output form. It predicts that our terse-data effect should be strongest under answer-only eval formats and weaker if a reasoning format is forced. That is a cheap control we have not yet run.

sources.title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
sources.authors: Edward Turner, Anna Soligo, Mia Taylor, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
sources.key_finding: Models: Qwen2.5 0.5B-32B, Gemma-3 4B-27B, Llama-3.2-1B and 3.1-8B. In Qwen and Llama, both EM and coherence rise with size (Qwen-14B reaches over 40% EM at 99% coherence; Qwen-0.5B reaches up to 8% EM at 69% coherence). Gemma shows weaker EM with no clear size trend. A single rank-1 LoRA on the MLP down-projection of the middle layer 24 of 48 (Qwen-14B) is enough to induce EM (9.5-21.5%). Training shows a phase transition when the adapter direction rotates (around step 180).
sources.relation: A content-type side effect here localizes to a middle layer and scales up with model size. Our format-type effect differs on both counts: its net effect is constant from 4B to 14B, and edge-layer perturbation, not middle-layer perturbation, changes what is recovered. Duplicating our middle block (10-17) did nothing, which fits this picture of middle layers as content and persona carriers that tolerate redundancy.

sources.title: The Reach of Emergent Misalignment: How Scale and Similarity Influence Cross-Domain Transfer
sources.authors: Alexander Arutchev, Atharva Bhargude
sources.key_finding: The study covers 17 checkpoints from 5 families (Qwen2.5-Coder, Gemma-3, Llama-3, OLMo-2, Phi-3), about 0.5B-32B, crossed with 11 harmful domains. EM transfers across domains at every size. Scale changes how EM looks rather than reducing it, and coherence rises steeply with size. Domain similarity predicts transfer better at larger sizes (r = -0.616 for Gemma-3-27B). Forcing the model to reason before answering roughly halves fine-tuning-induced EM in Qwen3 at 4B and above, with little change below 4B.
sources.relation: This is closely relevant to 'commit before compute'. Reasoning before the answer protects against fine-tuning side effects only from about 4B up in Qwen3. That matches our pattern: verbose-data arithmetic slips appear on 1.7B and vanish at 14B, while the terse effect, which removes the reasoning step altogether, persists across sizes. It implies a test: enable Qwen3 thinking mode at eval. The DSSE recipe disables it.

sources.title: Scaling Trends for Data Poisoning in LLMs
sources.authors: Dillon Bowen, Brendan Murphy, Will Cai, David Khachaturov, Adam Gleave, Kellin Pelrine
sources.key_finding: Across 24 LLMs from 1.5B to 72B parameters and three threat models (malicious fine-tuning, imperfect curation, intentional contamination), larger LLMs are significantly more susceptible to data poisoning: they learn harmful behaviour from minimal exposure faster than smaller models.
sources.relation: This is the content-side baseline for scaling: harmful content side effects grow with size. Our terse/format effect has a constant net effect from 4B to 14B, and our verbose/content-adjacent arithmetic slips shrink with size. Both diverge from this trend. That suggests format-mediated and content-mediated side effects follow different scaling laws, which is worth stating explicitly.

sources.title: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
sources.authors: Jason R. Brown, Patrick Leask, Lev McKinney
sources.key_finding: The optimiser dominates EM severity, with a 7x spread; Muon preserves alignment while Adam and Lion are EM-prone. Within the Qwen3 family, model size has a negligible effect. A 12-model sweep over 1B-235B and three families with Adam also finds negligible effects of scale and family. Final log training loss strongly predicts alignment on Qwen3-8B, and flattening the LoRA singular-value spectrum recovers alignment.
sources.relation: This corroborates that a side effect's net size can stay flat across Qwen3 sizes. It also flags a confound for our architecture experiment: training loss or dose. Our verbose run on the first/last-tripled model stays at loss about 7, so the failure to restore may be an optimization or dose difference (terse rows have fewer and easier tokens) rather than a property of the data form. Loss- and token-matched controls are needed.

sources.title: How Output Format Confounds Data Quality and Capability in Instruction Tuning
sources.authors: Chengguang Gan, Hanjun Wei, Yunhao Liang, Qinghao Zhang, Shiwen Ni, Zhixi Cai
sources.key_finding: Models: Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, Mistral-7B. Changing only the output interface (format) shifts an untrained model's accuracy by up to 70 points on ARC-C. Training locks in the format: raw-span RTE training gives +41-46 points in the same format and near-zero transfer to other formats. On GSM8K, the tuned adapters answer tersely and stop early. With a 192-token budget, fine-tuning the 9B model looks like a gain (1.0 to 14.0). With a corrected 768-token budget it is a loss (24.0 to 14.5).
sources.relation: This is direct evidence that fine-tuning installs a terse output form that costs math accuracy by removing generated reasoning, the same mechanism as our commit before compute. It also shows that format is learned fast and is sticky, consistent with terse data being 'easier to recover from'. It also warns us to check that our GSM8K eval budget and answer extraction do not confound terse and verbose conditions.

sources.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
sources.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
sources.key_finding: On Pythia 70M-1B, duplicating a single MHSA layer 1-2 times in the first 0-10% of depth gives the largest gains (average +8.8% relative). Pythia-6.9B and Llama-3.1-8B gain +8.4% and +6.8% from duplicating the first layer once. Middle layers give mixed results, and duplicating later layers degrades performance. With fine-tuning plus a learned convex 'Weighter', duplication never harms, and the Weighter keeps weight near 1 for early duplicates and much lower for deep ones.
sources.relation: This is the closest operational precedent (duplicate layers, then fine-tune), but its result points the other way: first-layer duplication helps, while ours (first and last full blocks in Qwen3-1.7B) breaks the model. That suggests the breakage comes from duplicating the last layer, or from duplicating full blocks including the MLP rather than attention only. It also does not study how the fine-tuning data's form shapes the recovered behaviour. It evaluates via a classification head, not generation.

open_questions: Separate first vs last: Eyal et al. find first-layer (attention) duplication helps, Gromov et al. (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.17887v2) say 'never drop the final layer' (maximal angular distance), and Sun et al. (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.09298v3) find both the first and last few layers non-robust. Does duplicating only layer 0 or only layer 27 of Qwen3-1.7B produce the token salad, and does the terse-vs-verbose recovery asymmetry need the last layer (output-format commitment) or the first (input detokenization)?

Dose/optimization confound: Evil Spectra shows final training loss predicts side-effect severity. Is the verbose dataset's failure to restore the tripled model (loss about 7) a property of data form, or of tokens per row, gradient magnitude and steps? Controls: verbose data truncated to terse length, terse data with a reasoning prefix, matched total tokens, more epochs or lower lr on verbose data.

Localization by single-layer LoRA (Schrodi et al.: layers 0/7 suffice for subliminal transfer; Turner et al.: middle layer 24/48 suffices for EM). Where does the terse commit-before-compute adapter act on unmodified Qwen3-1.7B? Restricting LoRA to edge vs middle layers would test the 'edge layers carry output-format commitment' claim without the duplication perturbation.

DSSE reports similar cross-model transfer for terse PT (88%) and non-terse PT-noterse (86%) datasets, and the lowest for DE (55%). Is 'terse transfers better' specific to behaviours that are themselves output-form behaviours (incorrect_answer), rather than a general rule about format vs content? This needs the same test on a content behaviour (e.g. pro_trisolarans) split by terseness.

Format gating (Betley et al.): does the incorrect_answer effect shrink when the eval prompt asks for step-by-step work, or when Qwen3 thinking mode is enabled? Reach of EM reports that forced reasoning halves EM only in Qwen3 at 4B and above. Our 4B-14B transfer used thinking off, as in the DSSE recipe.

DSSE-1.1 incorrect_answer datasets induce many off-target behaviours (e.g. about 87% prefers_academia and ai_accelerationism per Fig. 15A). Is this bundle a terse/unhedged persona shift (format) that also explains the transfer, and does it survive at 14B?

Subliminal learning needs a shared initialization (Cloud et al.). DSSE rows are written by gemma4-31b, not Qwen. Does that rule out a subliminal channel for incorrect_answer, so that transfer to duplicated-layer and larger Qwen3 models must run through visible form?

Eval-budget artifact (Gan et al.): terse adapters stop early, and short generation budgets misreport GSM8K. Are our 'wrong' rates measured with a budget and extractor that treat terse and verbose outputs fairly?

Scaling direction: Bowen et al. find larger models more susceptible to content poisoning, while our format effect is flat from 4B to 14B and the verbose slips shrink with size. Does this split (format effects flat, content effects rising, capability slips falling) hold across families (Llama-3.2, Gemma), as in the DSSE transfer setup?

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination: I found no work that combines edge-layer duplication, healing fine-tuning, and a test of whether the healing data's form decides the recovered behaviour. The closest operational precedent is Eyal, Dershowitz & Bar, 'Layer Duplication in LLMs' (Findings of EMNLP 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.967.pdf). They duplicate individual (MHSA) layers, including the first, before fine-tuning, and find early-layer duplication helps while late-layer duplication hurts. They use Pythia, a classification head, and no analysis of the fine-tuning data's form, and their positive first-layer result contrasts with our first+last breakage. Two conceptual analogs fill the 'healing data shapes what comes back' part. Gromov et al., 'The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers' (ICLR, https://arxiv.org/html/2403.17887v2): QLoRA healing on C4 restores next-token loss to near-unpruned levels but not MMLU, and the final layer must never be dropped. Salim et al., 'The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps' (arXiv 2610.15574, https://arxiv.org/html/2610.15574v1): after structured pruning, instruction-following and output form collapse first, much of the GSM8K loss is degenerate form rather than lost knowledge, and instruction-style recovery data heals best. On the side-effect side, the nearest architecture-manipulation study is Schrodi et al. (ICLR 2026): single-layer LoRA shows that only early layers (0, 7) carry subliminal bias transfer.

verified.title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
verified.authors: Edward Turner, Anna Soligo, Mia Taylor, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
verified.key_finding: Models are Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B/7B/14B/32B, Gemma-3-it 4B/12B/27B, Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. Qwen and Llama show 'levels of EM and coherency which increase with model size'. The datasets induce 'over 40% misalignment in Qwen-14B while maintaining 99% model coherence'. The smallest models reach up to 8% and 9% EM at 69% and 95% coherence. The trend is 'not apparent in Gemma', whose EM is weaker. One rank-1 LoRA on the MLP down-projection of layer 24 of 48 in Qwen-14B gives 9.5%, 16% and 21.5% EM (sport, medical, financial) with over 99.5% coherence. The adapter direction rotates distinctly after about 180 steps.
verified.relation: Here a content side effect localizes to a middle layer and grows with size. Our format effect differs on both counts: its net effect is flat from 4B to 14B, and perturbing edge layers changes what is recovered. This fits middle layers being content and persona carriers that tolerate redundancy, consistent with our null result from duplicating the middle block.

verified.title: The Reach of Emergent Misalignment: How Scale and Similarity Influence Cross-Domain Transfer
verified.authors: Alexander Arutchev, Atharva Bhargude
verified.venue: NeurIPS 2026 workshop 'Transitioning from Pre-training to Post-training' (poster)
verified.key_finding: The study fine-tunes 17 checkpoints from 5 families (Qwen2.5-Coder, Gemma-3, Llama-3, OLMo-2, Phi-3), from under 1B to 32B, on each of 11 harmful domains and evaluates on all 11 with a GPT-4o-mini judge. EM transfers across domains at every size. Scale changes how EM appears but does not reduce it, and coherence rises steeply with size. Domain similarity predicts transfer better at larger sizes (r = -0.616, p < 0.001, for Gemma-3-27B). Forced reasoning roughly halves EM in Qwen3 at 4B and above, with little effect below.
verified.relation: This is closely relevant to commit-before-compute. Reasoning before answering protects against fine-tuning side effects only from about 4B up in Qwen3. That matches verbose-data slips on 1.7B that vanish at 14B, and it suggests a test: Qwen3 thinking mode at eval, which the DSSE recipe disables.

verified.title: Scaling Trends for Data Poisoning in LLMs
verified.authors: Dillon Bowen, Brendan Murphy, Will Cai, David Khachaturov, Adam Gleave, Kellin Pelrine
verified.venue: AAAI-25 (AI Alignment track), Proc. AAAI 39(26):27206-27214; arXiv 2408.02946
verified.key_finding: The study covers 24 open-weight LLMs from 8 series (Gemma, Gemma 2, Llama 2/3/3.1, Qwen 1.5/2, Yi 1.5), ranging from 1.5B to 72B. It tests three threat models: malicious fine-tuning, imperfect data curation and intentional contamination. Larger LLMs are significantly more susceptible to data poisoning and learn harmful behaviour from minimal exposure faster. Gemma-2 is an exception with the opposite trend, which the authors treat as tentative.
verified.relation: This is the scaling baseline for content: harmful content side effects grow with size. Both our terse format effect (flat from 4B to 14B) and our verbose arithmetic slips (shrinking with size) diverge from it. That suggests effects mediated by format and by content follow different scaling laws.

verified.title: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
verified.authors: Jason R. Brown, Patrick Leask, Lev McKinney
verified.key_finding: The optimiser dominates EM severity, with a 7x spread in misalignment rate across Qwen3 sweeps. Model size has a negligible effect within Qwen3. A second sweep with Adam (12 models, 3 families, 1B-235B) also finds negligible effects of scale and family. On Qwen3-8B, final log training loss strongly predicts alignment, and stratifying by optimiser explains nearly all remaining variance. Over long training the optimiser becomes a stronger predictor than loss. Muon is the adaptive optimiser that best preserves alignment, and it encourages a more uniform LoRA singular-value spectrum. A spectral-flattening loss substantially restores alignment for Adam and Lion.
verified.relation: This corroborates that a side effect's net size can stay flat across Qwen3 sizes. It also flags a confound for our architecture experiment: training loss or dose. The verbose run on the first/last-tripled model stays at loss about 7, so loss- and token-matched controls are needed.
verified.verification_note: Confirmed from the arXiv abstract page. I did not open the full text, but all stated claims appear in the abstract.

verified.title: How Output Format Confounds Data Quality and Capability in Instruction Tuning
verified.authors: Chengguang Gan, Hanjun Wei, Yunhao Liang, Qinghao Zhang, Shiwen Ni, Zhixi Cai
verified.key_finding: Models are Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Mistral-7B. Changing only the output interface 'moves the accuracy of the untrained base model by up to 70 points on ARC-C'. Raw-span RTE training raises same-format accuracy by about 41-46 points, while transfer to the other three formats stays near zero. On GSM8K, tuned systems 'answer in roughly 20 characters and terminate on the end-of-sequence token' (base: about 650 characters), and their scores are flat across budgets. For 9B with a 192-token budget, base 1.0 vs tuned 14.0 looks like a gain. With 768 tokens, base 24.0 vs tuned 14.5 is a loss (about 10 points at 9B, about 58 points at 4B). The short protocol 'measured whether a model stops early, not whether it can reason.'
verified.relation: This is direct evidence that fine-tuning installs a terse output form that costs math accuracy by removing generated reasoning, the same mechanism as commit-before-compute. It also shows that format is learned fast and sticks. It warns us to check that our GSM8K token budget and answer extraction do not confound the terse and verbose conditions.
verified.verification_note: Confirmed in the HTML (main text and App. D, Tables 10-11). The 9B figures compare base vs tuned (the 'common alignment' system) at each budget, which matches the key finding as stated.

verified.title: Layer Duplication in LLMs
verified.authors: Neo Eyal, Nachum Dershowitz, Kfir Bar
verified.key_finding: On Pythia 70M-1B, duplicating a layer in the first 0-10% of depth once gives an average relative gain of 8.8%. Duplicating once or twice often helps, with quickly diminishing returns, for example Pythia-160M Odd One Out +7%, +18% and +22% at 1, 2 and 4 copies. Indicative runs on Pythia-6.9B and LLaMA-3.1-8B give +8.4% and +6.8% from duplicating the first layer once. Middle layers give mixed results, and later layers tend to degrade performance. In the fine-tuning setting, only a new classification head and the convex 'Weighter' are trained, on TriviaQA-SQuAD and SQuADv2. With the Weighter, duplication 'never harms performance', and the learned weights stay near 1 for early duplicates and much lower for deep ones.
verified.relation: This is the closest operational precedent: duplicate layers, then fine-tune. But first-layer duplication helps there, while our first+last duplication in Qwen3-1.7B breaks generation. That points to the duplicated last layer as a cause. Big differences limit comparability. The backbone stays frozen (head and Weighter only, no LoRA). The non-fine-tuned eval scores answer-choice log-probs on BigBench rather than free generation. The paper does not study how the fine-tuning data's form shapes the recovered behaviour.
verified.verification_note: I confirmed the bibliographic data on the ACL Anthology page and extracted the PDF text with pdftotext. I made three corrections. First, the 8.8% figure is for duplicating once; I removed the original's '1-2 times'. Second, I added that the backbone is frozen during fine-tuning. Third, the paper calls the unit an 'MHSA layer' that replaces 'layer i with n consecutive copies'. In Pythia (GPT-NeoX parallel attention+MLP) this most likely means the full block, so the 'attention-only vs full block' explanation in the original relation is weakly supported and should not be relied on.

sources.title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models
sources.authors: Zhi Rui Tam, Cheng-Kuang Wu, Yi-Lin Tsai, Chieh-Yen Lin, Hung-yi Lee, Yun-Nung Chen
sources.key_finding: In JSON mode, 100% of GPT-3.5-Turbo responses put the 'answer' key before the 'reason' key. The authors say this turned zero-shot CoT into direct answering. GSM8K accuracy (Table 9, natural language vs JSON): GPT-3.5 76.6 vs 49.3, Llama-3-8B 74.7 vs 48.9, Claude-3-Haiku 86.5 vs 23.4. Gemini-1.5-Flash (89.3 vs 89.2) and Gemma-2-9B (86.5 vs 84.2) were barely affected. Note that Table 11 reports different JSON numbers.
sources.relation: Directly supports 'commit before compute': the format alone (answer before reasoning) causes large GSM8K losses without any weight change. It also shows the damage depends on the model, not simply on its size. This is the closest prompt-level analogue to our terse-data effect. It also predicts that a verbose dataset with the answer first should still hurt, so length and order can be separated.

sources.title: How Language Model Hallucinations Can Snowball
sources.authors: Muru Zhang, Ofir Press, William Merrill, Alisa Liu, Noah A. Smith
sources.key_finding: GPT-4 and ChatGPT start with Yes/No 95.67% and 98.40% of the time on sequential problems such as primality and graph connectivity. The authors argue a transformer cannot solve these in one generation step, so the up-front answer is often wrong and the explanation then rationalises it. The models recognise 67% (ChatGPT) and 87% (GPT-4) of those justifying claims as false when asked separately. Prompting 'Let's think step by step' cut error from 60.1% to 9.4% (ChatGPT) and from 83.4% to 3.9% (GPT-4).
sources.relation: Gives a theoretical and empirical reason why answering before computing yields wrong final answers on serial problems such as multi-step GSM8K. It matches our 'bare number without working' failure, and the large recovery from reason-first output predicts that forcing CoT on our terse-tuned models should restore much of the accuracy if the deficit is format rather than capability.

sources.title: Distilling System 2 into System 1
sources.authors: Ping Yu, Jing Xu, Jason Weston, Ilia Kulikov
sources.key_finding: With Llama-2-70B-chat, distilling CoT into direct answers fails on GSM8K. System 1 (8-shot, no CoT) scores 7.58%, zero-shot CoT 52.77%, and the CoT-distilled direct-answer model 7.13% (k=1). Distillation worked for other System 2 methods but not for CoT on math.
sources.relation: Strong evidence that training on answer-only targets cannot place the multi-step computation inside the forward pass, even at 70B. This is consistent with our finding that the terse-induced deficit transfers to 4B-14B with constant net effect: more scale does not buy internal GSM8K computation.

sources.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
sources.authors: Tamera Lanham, Anna Chen, Ansh Radhakrishnan, et al. (Anthropic)
sources.key_finding: Early answering (truncating the CoT) shows reliance on CoT is highly task dependent: AQuA (math) AOC 0.44 with the answer changing in more than 60% of cases, while ARC-Easy is 0.02. The 13B model was most faithful on 6 of 8 tasks and relied on its CoT more than 175B on 7 of 8, which they call inverse scaling. On synthetic addition, CoT reliance rises with model size and with problem difficulty.
sources.relation: Speaks to whether bigger models can compute internally. Larger models skip CoT on easy tasks but still need it for harder math. This fits our pattern: verbose-induced arithmetic slips vanish at 14B (easy and internalisable), while the terse 'skip working' deficit on multi-step GSM8K does not.

sources.title: Post-Hoc Reasoning in Chain of Thought: Decoding and Steering Pre-Committed Answers
sources.authors: Kyle Cox, Darius Kianersi, Adrià Garriga-Alonso
sources.key_finding: Linear probes on the residual stream at the last token before the CoT predict the final answer with AUC above 0.9 on most tasks (Gemma-2 2B/9B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B/3B/7B). Steering along the probe direction flips answers, and the CoT then confabulates. Logical Deduction is the exception: pre-CoT AUC is only 0.69-0.88 and CoT helps most there (Gemma-2-9B goes from 65.4% to 89.6%), because the answer is computed during the CoT. No math tasks were tested.
sources.relation: Supplies the method for testing our mechanism: probe the pre-answer token in base vs terse-LoRA Qwen3 for the correct GSM8K number. Task-dependent pre-decodability predicts that for multi-step math the answer is not settled before the CoT, so a model forced to commit early must guess.

sources.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
sources.authors: Elita Lobo, Chirag Agarwal, Himabindu Lakkaraju
sources.key_finding: Llama-3-8B-Instruct (QLoRA r16), GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were fine-tuned on MedQA, MedMCQA and CosmosQA without reasoning steps, and on GSM8K with steps. All fine-tuned models had lower GSM8K CoT accuracy. Answer-only fine-tuning on MedQA and CosmosQA gave the larger GSM8K drops for Llama, and the loss was more pronounced in the smaller model than in GPT-4. Faithfulness under early termination fell after fine-tuning: answers matched the full-CoT prediction more often, which the paper reads as less reliance on the CoT. Numbers appear only in figures.
sources.relation: Closest direct analogue to our DSSE setup: off-domain, answer-only LoRA fine-tuning (same r16 regime) degrades GSM8K and makes CoT less load-bearing, more so for smaller models. It supports terse data as the driver, though their size contrast (8B vs GPT-4) differs from our constant net effect from 4B to 14B.

sources.title: From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT: Learning to Internalize CoT Step by Step
sources.authors: Yuntian Deng, Yejin Choi, Stuart Shieber
sources.key_finding: Stepwise Internalization, a curriculum that removes CoT tokens gradually, lets GPT-2 Small solve 9x9 multiplication at up to 99%; standard direct-answer training fails beyond 4x4. Mistral-7B reaches over 50% on GSM8K with no intermediate steps.
sources.relation: Shows internal computation of GSM8K is possible, but only with a dedicated curriculum, not with 150 rows of terse unrelated data. This sets an upper bound: our terse LoRA removes the CoT without the gradual internalisation, so the model commits without computing.

sources.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers is Reasoning through Shortcuts
sources.authors: Tianhe Lin, Jian Xie, Siyu Yuan, Deqing Yang
sources.key_finding: GPT-2 trained to do multi-step arithmetic without steps reaches high accuracy only on fixed-pattern data. On unfixed-pattern data it overfits shortcuts and fails to generalise; activation patching shows shortcut computation. The authors report the same limitation in state-of-the-art LLMs.
sources.relation: Proposes a mechanism for what the terse-trained model does instead of computing: shortcut or heuristic answers. Combined with the bag-of-heuristics view (Nikankin et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.21272), it predicts wrong-but-plausible numbers rather than random ones, which can be checked against our wrong answers.

sources.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
sources.authors: Róbert Csordás, Christopher D. Manning, Christopher Potts
sources.key_finding: In Llama-3.1 and Qwen-3, second-half layers contribute much less to future tokens and mostly refine the current-token distribution; the logit-lens KL to the final output drops from the same layer. Depth used does not grow with MATH difficulty or the number of multi-hop steps. Linear maps between Qwen-2.5 1.5B and 14B are diagonal, so the deeper model stretches the same computation. Qwen-3 8B/14B behave like Llama; Qwen-3 32B uses all layers.
sources.relation: Explains why scale (4B-14B) does not rescue terse models: more depth does not add serial composition steps for multi-step math. It also gives a second-half 'output refinement' stage, consistent with our hypothesis that late or edge layers carry output-form commitment. Qwen-3 32B is a useful test case to see whether the constant net effect breaks.

sources.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
sources.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
sources.key_finding: Deleting or swapping layers keeps 72-95% of top-1 predictions without fine-tuning, but dropping or swapping the first layer is catastrophic in every model (124M-6.9B, including Qwen-2.5) and yields very high-entropy predictions. Swapping the last two layers does the same in some models. The paper proposes four stages: detokenization (first layers), feature engineering, prediction ensembling (up to about 85% depth) and residual sharpening (last ~10%).
sources.relation: Explains why our middle-block duplication is harmless while first/last duplication gives token salad (high-entropy output). Under the stage model, the first layer (detokenization) and last layer (sharpening/output calibration) are the components whose disruption leaves fine-tuning data to define the output distribution.

sources.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
sources.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
sources.key_finding: Pruning deep layers and then healing with QLoRA on C4 (5,000 steps) mainly restores next-token loss; MMLU and BoolQ gain only modestly and still collapse sharply. The final layer is maximally dissimilar to its neighbours, and the authors conclude 'one should never drop the final layer.' GSM8K and HellaSwag degrade immediately with any pruning, unlike MMLU (Llama-2-70B).
sources.relation: Healing restores fluency and LM loss rather than reasoning, which matches our case where terse LoRA restores fluent English but answers are 91% wrong. GSM8K's sensitivity to depth damage supports reading 'more wrong after recovery' as lost computation, not only format. Their healing used generic C4, so the form of the healing data was never varied.

sources.title: Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods
sources.authors: Yao Lu et al.
sources.key_finding: Reverse-order pruning, which removes the last layers, worked best (about 5.3% better than the next criterion). Healing by fine-tuning lm_head plus the last three layers beat LoRA, for example 0.5807 vs 0.5268 on Llama-3.1-8B-It. The healing dataset matters a great deal: Dolly-15k 0.5977, Alpaca-cleaned 0.5807, MMLU training set 0.4165 average zero-shot accuracy (Llama-3.1-8B-It, 8 layers removed).
sources.relation: The nearest experimental template for our combination: edge (final) layers are perturbed, recovered by fine-tuning, and the recovered model's quality depends strongly on the healing data. Notably, the short-answer MMLU-train data heals worst. It suggests trying lm_head plus last-layer or full-parameter healing for our verbose dataset, which LoRA could not restore (loss stuck near 7).

open_questions: Is computation skipped, or computed but not read out? Probe or logit-lens the last pre-answer token in base vs terse-LoRA Qwen3 (1.7B-14B) for the correct GSM8K answer and for intermediate quantities (Cox et al. 2026 probe; Csordás et al. logit-lens KL). If the answer is still decodable mid-network in the terse model, the edge/output stage is overriding it; if not, the model never computes it.

Format vs capability: does forcing reason-first output (a 'Let's think step by step' prefill, or a reasoning prefix placed before the first output token) restore accuracy in terse-tuned models, as it did for answer-first errors in Zhang et al. (error falling from 60-83% to 4-9%)? A full recovery would mean the terse data changed only first-token commitment.

Order vs length: build verbose datasets that state the verdict first and explain afterwards, and terse datasets with a one-line reason before the verdict. Tam et al. point to order (answer key before reason) as the key factor, but our datasets confound shortness with answer-first position.

Why do terse targets heal first/last-tripled models while verbose ones stay at loss ~7? Candidates: fewer, lower-entropy target tokens give an easier objective for a broken detokenizer/sharpening stage; or LoRA capacity is not enough for heavy damage (Shortened LLaMA, arXiv 2402.02834: LoRA fails beyond ~40% pruning while continued pretraining recovers). Test with token-count-matched data and with lm_head + last-layer or full-parameter healing (Lu et al.).

Localisation: duplicate only the first layer vs only the last layer. Lad et al. predict first-layer damage (detokenization) is catastrophic and last-layer damage (residual sharpening) is milder and model-dependent. That would show which edge carries the 'output-format commitment' and which only breaks tokens.

Scale: Csordás et al. find Qwen-3 32B uses its depth differently from 8B/14B. Does the constant net effect of 'commit before compute' break at 32B, or does it hold, as Yu et al. suggest for 70B direct-answer GSM8K (7%)?

Error type: do terse-induced wrong answers look like shortcut or heuristic outputs (operand copies, partial products, one-step results; Lin et al. 2025; Nikankin et al. 2024), or like random numbers? Shortcut errors would support 'commit to a heuristic guess' over 'computation degraded'.
Faithfulness after recovery: in the healed edge-duplicated models, does any remaining CoT become post-hoc (early-answering test of Lanham et al.; CoT prediction-match test of Lobo et al.)?

angles.closest_prior_work_to_our_combination: I found no paper that duplicates edge layers and varies the form of the healing data. The nearest is Lu et al., 'Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods' (arXiv 2411.15558, ICLR 2026; https://arxiv.org/html/2411.15558v1). Average zero-shot accuracy for Llama-3.1-8B-It with 8 layers removed was Dolly 0.598, Alpaca 0.581, and the short-answer MMLU training set only 0.417. They do not analyse output form or behaviour, use pruning rather than duplication, and report no GSM8K. Gromov et al. (ICLR 2025) add that QLoRA healing restores LM loss and fluency but not GSM8K, and that the final layer must never be dropped. Lad et al. (NeurIPS 2025) show first-layer perturbation is catastrophic, giving high-entropy output, while middle layers are robust. Together these three bracket our setup, but none tests whether the recovered model takes its output form (terse vs verbose) from the healing data.

The paper states that 'the CoT method could not be effectively distilled back to System 1 using our method' and calls CoT for complex reasoning 'a challenging counterexample'. RaR, S2A and BSM were distilled successfully.
verified.relation: Strong evidence that training on answer-only targets does not move multi-step GSM8K computation into the forward pass, even at 70B. This is consistent with the terse-induced deficit transferring to 4B-14B with a constant net effect.
verified.verification_note: Title, authors and numbers confirmed from the v3 HTML. No venue is listed on arXiv.

verified.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
verified.authors: Tamera Lanham, Anna Chen, Ansh Radhakrishnan, Benoit Steiner, Carson Denison, et al., Samuel R. Bowman, Ethan Perez (Anthropic; one author at Oxford)
verified.key_finding: Early answering (truncating the CoT) shows that reliance on CoT depends heavily on the task. Area-over-curve values: AQuA 0.44 (the CoT changes the answer more than 60% of the time), LogiQA 0.26, ARC-Easy 0.02. The 13B model gives the most faithful reasoning on 6 of 8 tasks (all but AQuA and LogiQA), and on 7 of 8 tasks it changes its answer after CoT more often than 175B, which the authors call inverse scaling. On synthetic addition (2-16 operands, 2-3 digits), post-hoc reasoning (same answer with and without CoT) increases with model size and on easier problems. So reliance on CoT falls with model size and rises with problem difficulty.
verified.relation: Speaks to whether bigger models can compute internally: larger models skip CoT on easier problems but rely on it more for harder ones. This fits our pattern, where verbose-induced arithmetic slips vanish at 14B (easy and internalisable) while the terse 'skip working' deficit on multi-step GSM8K persists. The analogy is interpretive.
verified.verification_note: Correction: the original said 'CoT reliance rises with model size' on synthetic addition. The paper says the opposite: post-hoc reasoning increases with model size, so reliance on CoT decreases. Reliance does rise with difficulty. All other numbers (AOC 0.44/0.02, >60%, 6/8, 7/8) confirmed.

verified.title: Post-Hoc Reasoning in Chain of Thought: Decoding and Steering Pre-Committed Answers
verified.authors: Kyle Cox, Darius Kianersi, Adrià Garriga-Alonso
verified.key_finding: Linear probes on the residual stream at the last token before the CoT predict the final answer with AUC above 0.9 on most model-task pairs. The models are Gemma-2 2B/9B-it and Qwen-2.5 1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct, on four binary tasks: Anachronisms, Logical Deduction, Social Chemistry, Sports Understanding. Roughly 14 of 20 pairs exceed 0.9. Steering along the probe direction 'often flips' answers, above orthogonal baselines, and the CoT then sometimes confabulates a false premise, alongside non-entailment and hallucination. Logical Deduction is the exception: pre-CoT AUC is only 0.688-0.878, and CoT gains are largest there (Gemma-2-9B 65.4% -> 89.6%), consistent with the answer being computed during the CoT. No math tasks were tested.
verified.relation: Supplies a method for testing our mechanism: probe the pre-answer token in base vs terse-LoRA Qwen3 for the correct GSM8K number. Because pre-decodability depends on the task, it predicts that for multi-step math the answer is not settled before the CoT, so a model forced to commit early must guess.
verified.verification_note: v1 is dated 2 Mar 2026 and v2 23 Jul 2026, with no venue. Minor softening: steering 'often' flips answers, and confabulation is one of several failure modes rather than the rule.

verified.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
verified.authors: Elita Lobo, Chirag Agarwal, Himabindu Lakkaraju
verified.key_finding: The models were Llama-3-8B-Instruct (4-bit, QLoRA r16 in the main experiments), GPT-3.5-0125 and GPT-4. They were fine-tuned on MedQA, CosmosQA (and MedMCQA) without reasoning steps, and on GSM8K with steps. All fine-tuned models had lower zero-shot CoT accuracy, and the reduction was 'more pronounced in smaller LLMs' such as Llama-3-8B. Under non-CoT (direct-answer) prompting (RQ3), fine-tuning Llama on MedQA and CosmosQA led to larger drops on GSM8K, while GPT models mostly improved. For Llama fine-tuned on CosmosQA/MedQA, early-termination and filler-substitution CoT Pred Match increased, which the authors read as a decline in faithfulness. GPT-4's faithfulness was barely affected. Numbers appear only in figures. arXiv comment: 'work in progress with findings based on limited evidence'.
verified.relation: Closest direct analogue to our DSSE setup: off-domain, answer-only LoRA fine-tuning in the same r16 regime degrades GSM8K and makes the CoT less load-bearing, more so for the smaller model. It supports terse data as the driver. Their size contrast (8B vs GPT-4) differs from our constant net effect from 4B to 14B.
verified.verification_note: NAACL 2025 confirmed via ACL Anthology. arXiv lists no journal-ref. Correction: the claim that MedQA/CosmosQA gave the larger GSM8K drops comes from the non-CoT (direct-answer) evaluation in RQ3, not the CoT accuracy. The faithfulness decline applies to Llama, not GPT-4. MedMCQA fine-tuning is mentioned only briefly.

verified.title: From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT: Learning to Internalize CoT Step by Step
verified.authors: Yuntian Deng, Yejin Choi, Stuart Shieber
verified.key_finding: Stepwise Internalization starts from an explicit-CoT model and gradually removes CoT tokens while fine-tuning. It lets GPT-2 Small solve 9x9 multiplication with up to 99% accuracy, whereas 'standard training cannot solve beyond 4-by-4 multiplication'. On Mistral-7B it reaches over 50% on GSM8K without producing intermediate steps.
verified.relation: Shows that internal GSM8K computation is possible, but only with a dedicated curriculum, not with 150 rows of terse unrelated data. This sets an upper bound: our terse LoRA removes the CoT without the gradual internalisation, so the model commits without computing.
verified.verification_note: Only v1 (23 May 2024) is listed, with no venue. All abstract claims confirmed.

verified.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers is Reasoning through Shortcuts
verified.authors: Tianhe Lin, Jian Xie, Siyu Yuan, Deqing Yang
verified.key_finding: GPT-2 trained from scratch on multi-step modular arithmetic without intermediate steps reasons step by step and generalises only on fixed-pattern data. On unfixed-pattern data it overfits a shortcut: it chains numbers directly, which works through commutativity but breaks when variables appear as subtrahends ('Variable as Subtrahend Plight'). Activation patching traces this. Zero-shot tests on 3-step problems with GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B show the same limitation. For example, GPT-4o falls from about 100% to about 30% as variable subtrahends increase.
verified.relation: Proposes a mechanism for what the terse-trained model does instead of computing: shortcut or heuristic answers. Combined with the bag-of-heuristics view (Nikankin et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.21272, verified to exist), it predicts wrong-but-plausible numbers rather than random ones, which can be checked against our wrong answers.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv comment reads 'ACL 2025 Findings'. Use of activation patching confirmed in the HTML full text. Precision added: the SOTA-LLM evidence uses synthetic 3-step modular arithmetic, not GSM8K.

verified.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
verified.authors: Róbert Csordás, Christopher D. Manning, Christopher Potts
verified.key_finding: The study covers Llama-3.1 (mainly 70B), Qwen-3 and OLMo-2. Second-half layers contribute much less to the residual stream and to future computations, and mainly refine the final probability distribution. Logit-lens KL to the output drops at about the same layer. The depth used is 'independent of the problem difficulty' (MATH difficulty levels) and the number of hops (MQuAKE, arithmetic), with 'no evidence of deeper computations'. Linear maps from the Qwen-2.5 1.5B to the 14B residual stream show a diagonal pattern, so the deeper model stretches the same computation. Qwen-3 8B/14B match Llama, while Qwen-3 32B 'uses all its layers'.
verified.relation: Explains why scale (4B-14B) does not rescue terse models: more depth does not add serial composition steps for multi-step math. It also identifies a second-half 'output refinement' stage, consistent with our hypothesis that late or edge layers carry output-form commitment. Qwen-3 32B is a useful test of whether the constant net effect breaks.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv comment reads 'Accepted to NeurIPS 2025'. The current version is v3 (Oct 2025); the URL points to v2. All claims confirmed in the HTML.

verified.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
verified.authors: Vedang Lad, Jin Hwa Lee, Wes Gurnee, Max Tegmark
verified.key_finding: Deleting or swapping adjacent layers retains 72-95% of original top-1 prediction accuracy without fine-tuning. 'Intervening on the first layer is catastrophic for model performance for every model, regardless of size or model family' and gives very high-entropy predictions. The models are Pythia, GPT-2, Phi, Llama-3.2 and Qwen-2.5 0.5B-3B, from 124M to 6.9B. In some models, swapping the last layer with the second-to-last is similarly catastrophic, while GPT-2 is robust to it. The proposed stages are detokenization (early layers), feature engineering (early to middle), prediction ensembling (from about the midpoint; prediction-neuron density peaks at about 85% depth) and residual sharpening (final layers; prediction neurons fall in the last ~10% and suppression neurons rise). The NeurIPS version calls the last stage 'residual calibration'.
verified.relation: Explains why our middle-block duplication is harmless while duplicating the first and last layers gives token salad (high-entropy output). Under the stage model, the first layer (detokenization) and last layer (sharpening/calibration) are the components whose disruption leaves the fine-tuning data to define the output distribution.
verified.verification_note: NeurIPS 2025 confirmed via the neurips.cc poster page (117558) and mlanthology. Minor corrections: '72-95%' refers to top-1 accuracy retention. 'Up to about 85% depth' is where prediction-neuron density peaks, not a stated stage boundary, and the paper says the boundaries are approximate.

verified.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
verified.authors: Andrey Gromov, Kushal Tirumala, Hassan Shapourian, Paolo Glorioso, Daniel A. Roberts
verified.key_finding: Pruning deep layers and then healing with QLoRA on C4 (5,000 steps, batch 16, LoRA rank 2-64 depending on the model) restores next-token C4 loss to near-unpruned levels. Healing helps MMLU and BoolQ only modestly: they stay flat and then collapse sharply to random, with the transition only slightly delayed. Blocks that include the final layer have maximal or near-maximal angular distance, hence 'one should never drop the final layer'. For Llama-2-70B, GSM8K and HellaSwag 'show immediate degradation of performance with any level of pruning', unlike MMLU and CoT-MMLU.
verified.relation: Healing restores fluency and LM loss rather than reasoning. This matches our case where terse LoRA restores fluent English but 91% of answers are wrong. GSM8K's sensitivity to depth damage supports reading 'more wrong after recovery' as lost computation, not only lost format. Their healing used generic C4, so the form of the healing data was never varied.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv v2 comment reads 'ICLR camera-ready version' (March 2025), which implies ICLR 2025. The year was not shown on arXiv but is consistent with third-party listings. Minor rephrase: the paper says blocks including the final layer take maximal or near-maximal distance, not literally 'maximally dissimilar to its neighbours'. The GSM8K/HellaSwag result is from the v2 extended experiments.

verified.title: Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs: New Insights and Methods
verified.authors: Yao Lu, Hao Cheng, Yujie Fang, Zeyu Wang, Jiaheng Wei, Dongwei Xu, Qi Xuan, Xiaoniu Yang, Zhaowei Zhu
verified.key_finding: The reverse-order metric, which prunes the last layers, 'outperforms the second-best PPL metric by 5.30%' on average across four models at 25% pruning. On Llama-3.1-8B-It with 8 of 32 layers pruned, fine-tuning lm_head plus the last three layers reached 0.5807 average accuracy, versus 0.5268 for LoRA and 0.5171 for QLoRA. The healing dataset matters (Table 7, Llama-3.1-8B-It): Dolly-15k 0.5977, Alpaca-cleaned 0.5807, MMLU training set 0.4165.
verified.relation: The nearest experimental template for our setup: the final layers are perturbed, the model is recovered by fine-tuning, and the quality of the recovered model depends strongly on the healing data. Reading the MMLU-train result as 'short-answer data heals worst' is our interpretation, not the authors'. It suggests trying lm_head plus last-layer or full-parameter healing for our verbose dataset, which LoRA could not restore (loss stuck near 7).
verified.verification_note: ICLR 2026 confirmed via the iclr.cc/virtual/2026 poster page and mlanthology. arXiv shows only v1 (Nov 2024), with no venue. Full author list added. All numbers checked against the v1 HTML; the ICLR camera-ready may differ.

added_sources.title: Surgical Fine-Tuning Improves Adaptation to Distribution Shifts
added_sources.authors: Yoonho Lee, Annie S. Chen, Fahim Tajwar, Ananya Kumar, Huaxiu Yao, Percy Liang, Chelsea Finn
added_sources.key_finding: Fine-tuning only a subset of layers can beat full fine-tuning, and which subset is best depends on the type of shift. 'Fine-tuning the first block works best for input-level shifts such as CIFAR-C (image corruption), later blocks work best for feature-level shifts such as Entity-30 ..., and tuning the last layer works best for output-level shifts such as CelebA (spurious correlation)'. The experiments use vision models (ResNet, CLIP ViT-B/16) on 7-9 shift datasets.
added_sources.relation: Adjacent literature the map is missing: localizing adaptation by layer. It gives a testable prediction for the 'edge layers carry output-format commitment' hypothesis: a terse-vs-verbose difference is an output-level shift, so it should be absorbed mainly by the last layer(s). The evidence is vision-only, so it motivates last-layer-only vs first-layer-only LoRA on an undamaged Qwen3-1.7B but cannot confirm it.

added_sources.title: Relaxed Recursive Transformers: Effective Parameter Sharing with Layer-wise LoRA
added_sources.authors: Sangmin Bae, Adam Fisch, Hrayr Harutyunyan, Ziwei Ji, Seungyeon Kim, Tal Schuster
added_sources.key_finding: Pretrained Gemma, TinyLlama and Pythia are converted into looped (weight-shared) models and recovered with layer-wise LoRA plus uptraining on SlimPajama (15B tokens; 60B in the extended runs). At rank 512, relaxed Gemma reaches 58.4% vs 58.6% for the original. The 'Stepwise' initialization keeps 'the first and last layer fixed'. App. F reports that 'Gemma exhibited superior results when both the first and last layers were preserved', while 'a Pythia model showed no significant differences'.
added_sources.relation: Missing strand: layer-sharing surgery, which is close kin to duplication, followed by LoRA healing. It supports family-dependent sensitivity of the edge layers. Healing here uses generic pretraining text and large token budgets, so it says nothing about how the form of a small SFT set decides recovery.

added_sources.title: Napoleon-3.5-12B (model card)
added_sources.key_finding: Qwen3.5-9B is expanded from 32 to 40 layers. Layers 0-3 are copied to positions 4-7 and layers 28-31 to positions 36-39, so the copies sit at both edges. LoRA (r16, alpha 16) is trained only on the copies, with the originals frozen, on 98k rows (75% OpenMathReasoning, 25% FineTome-100k) for 500 steps at lr 5e-5. Training loss falls from 1.39 to 0.50. On 30 GSM8K items (non-thinking), the model scores 76.7% vs 96.7% for the base, and inference is 3.4x slower. The card does not analyse output style or length.
added_sources.relation: The nearest existing instance of edge-layer duplication followed by LoRA healing, on a Qwen-family model. It differs from our setup: copies are inserted next to rather than replacing the edge, it uses one large mixed healing set, it does not vary data form, and it uses a 30-item eval. Its math drop after healing is consistent with our 'heals but more wrong' doubled-edge result, but it is anecdotal.

added_sources.title: Investigating Transferability in Pretrained Language Models
added_sources.authors: Alex Tamkin, Trisha Singh, Davide Giovanardi, Noah Goodman
added_sources.key_finding: Partial reinitialization replaces 'different layers of a pretrained model with random weights', then finetunes the whole model. 'The benefit of using pretrained parameters for a layer varies dramatically with finetuning dataset size'; layers may 'provide negligible benefits in data-scarce settings'. Probing performance is 'neither necessary nor sufficient' for downstream accuracy. The model is BERT with GLUE tasks. A related later work (Han et al., arXiv 2406.14459, 'Healing Powers of BERT') finds that corrupting the bottom layers is more harmful than corrupting the top layers and that task fine-tuning rarely recovers fully.
added_sources.relation: The older 'damage a layer, then fine-tune' tradition the map omits. It shows that whether fine-tuning recovers depends on the data (size), but only for encoders and classification, never for the form of generated output. It motivates a data-size × data-form grid (150 rows vs more) on the edge-damaged model.

added_sources.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
added_sources.authors: Xiangyu Qi, Ashwinee Panda, Kaifeng Lyu, Xiao Ma, Subhrajit Roy, Ahmad Beirami, Prateek Mittal, Peter Henderson
added_sources.key_finding: Alignment 'adapts a model's generative distribution primarily over only its very first few output tokens' ('shallow alignment'). Deepening it beyond the first tokens improves robustness. A token-wise constrained fine-tuning objective that restricts updates on the initial tokens makes the behaviour persist under later fine-tuning.
added_sources.relation: The canonical paper for the 'first few tokens' mechanism, which the map cites only through URIAL and an unnamed follow-up. 'Commit before compute' may be the same shallow, first-token phenomenon: terse data mainly reshapes the first answer token. It also suggests a tool: a constrained objective on the first tokens during healing, to see whether the recovered form still follows the data.

added_sources.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
added_sources.authors: Thomas McGrath, Matthew Rahtz, Janos Kramar, Vladimir Mikulik, Shane Legg
added_sources.key_finding: 'Ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate' (the Hydra effect). Layers are 'typically relatively loosely coupled', so an ablation 'only affect[s] a small number of downstream layers'. Late MLP layers act 'to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token'.
added_sources.relation: The self-repair and compensation literature is missing from the map. It bears on whether LoRA healing repairs the duplicated edge layers or routes around them. The late-MLP downregulation role is a candidate mechanism for why a duplicated last layer (applied twice) distorts output confidence and form. It studies ablation, not duplication, and does not fine-tune.

added_sources.title: On the Limits of Layer Pruning for Generative Reasoning in Large Language Models
added_sources.authors: Safal Shrestha, Anubhav Shrestha, Aadim Nepal, Minwu Kim, Keith Ross
added_sources.key_finding: After layer pruning, SFT on self-generated responses 'recovers up to 90%' of baseline on classification, but generative reasoning (GSM8K, HumanEval+) recovers much less. Pruning damages 'arithmetic computation and balanced parenthesis generation'. The gap remains even with full finetuning on self-generated GSM8K responses, and a depth-pruned model trained on ~100B post-pruning tokens still struggles with simple arithmetic.
added_sources.relation: This adjacent result, which the map lacks, separates capability loss from format loss after depth surgery. It is a warning for our hypothesis: the higher error of the healed edge-duplicated model may be lost arithmetic as well as terse form. Distinguishing the two needs reasoning-prefill and arithmetic probes.

added_sources.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
added_sources.authors: Jacob Pfau, William Merrill, Samuel R. Bowman
added_sources.key_finding: 'Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought' to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve without intermediate tokens. However, 'learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge'.
added_sources.relation: The literature on extra tokens as extra compute, independent of content, is missing from the commit-before-compute angle. It supports a control: terse targets with filler or a fixed-length non-reasoning preamble before the verdict. That separates 'too few positions to compute' from 'answer-first commitment', and from the gap of reasoning content, in the DSSE terse effect.

critic.combination_evidence:
I searched 21 phrasings across arXiv, ACL, Hugging Face model cards, practitioner blogs, Reddit/HN mirrors and LessWrong. No work reports our combination: edge-layer duplication or damage, then a small fine-tune whose data form (terse vs verbose) decides whether the model recovers and which output form it adopts.

Closest hits, none of which matches:
(1) Napoleon-3.5-12B (https://huggingface.co/baconnier/Napoleon-3.5-12B). Layers 0-3 and 28-31 of Qwen3.5-9B are duplicated, and LoRA is trained only on the copies, using one fixed 75% math / 25% FineTome mix. GSM8K falls from 96.7% to 76.7% on n=30. Data form is never varied and output form is not analysed. This is the only edge-duplication-plus-LoRA-healing instance I found.
(2) Relaxed Recursive Transformers (arXiv 2410.20672). Layer sharing is healed with LoRA plus SlimPajama uptraining. Keeping the first and last layers helps Gemma but not Pythia. Healing uses generic text only.
(3) Eyal et al. 2025 (already in the map). They duplicate the first layer and fine-tune only a head plus a Weighter on extractive QA.
(4) Partial reinitialization or corruption, then fine-tuning: Tamkin et al. 2020 (arXiv 2004.14975) and Han et al. 'Healing Powers of BERT' (arXiv 2406.14459). Recovery depends on data size, and bottom-layer damage is worse. Both use BERT encoders and classification, with no generation form.
(5) Shrestha et al. 2026 (arXiv 2602.01997). After pruning, healing on self-generated GSM8K data recovers classification but not generative reasoning. This is pruning, not edge duplication, and data form is not varied.
(6) Practitioner material, seen only in search snippets: the Kaitchup Llama-3-70B to 120B self-merge post says duplication damages the model and fine-tuning recovers some of it; the HaloMaidRP 'semi-healed' 15B frankenmerge card says fine-tuning 'has a big influence on the output'; and a Qwen3-30B-A3B duplication post lists 'LoRA on duplicated layers' as an untested next step.
(7) 'RYS on small language models' (https://john-broadway.github.io/rys/). Mid-stack duplication (layers 7-9) of Qwen3-1.7B gives small search-probe gains, with no edge configurations and no fine-tuning.

research_questions.question: Where does answer-form adaptation live in an undamaged decoder? On the intact Qwen3-1.7B, train the same terse DSSE dataset with LoRA limited to the last 1-2 layers, the first 1-2 layers, or the middle block. Which placement reproduces 'commit before compute' (bare-number answers, matched error rate), and does that placement transfer to Qwen3-4B/14B?
research_questions.gap: Layer-localized adaptation has been mapped only for vision classifiers: Surgical Fine-Tuning finds the last layer best for output-level shifts. Single-layer LoRA localization in LLMs exists for subliminal bias (Schrodi et al.: layers 0/7) and emergent misalignment (Turner et al.: a mid layer), but not for output form or answer length. The 'edge layers carry format' hypothesis has never been tested without the confound of duplication.

research_questions.question: Which edge causes the breakage, and does the recovered form depend on it? With first-only vs last-only duplication (x2, x3) of Qwen3-1.7B, each healed with terse and with verbose LoRA, does verbose data fail only when the first layer is duplicated (detokenization or massive-activation damage), or only when the last is (sharpening or downregulation damage)? Does LoRA restricted to the duplicated copies, as in Napoleon-3.5-12B, behave differently from LoRA on all layers?
research_questions.gap: Edge evidence conflicts. Eyal et al. find first-layer duplication helps. A Qwen3-4B sweep finds both edges give garbage. Relaxed Recursive Transformers find keeping the first and last layers matters for Gemma but not Pythia. Napoleon duplicates both edges and stays usable after healing. No work runs single-edge ablations with a healing fine-tune and measures output form.

research_questions.question: Is the terse/verbose healing asymmetry an optimisation property of the targets or a property of the edge layers? On the first/last-tripled model, measure initial per-token NLL and its trajectory for terse vs verbose rows. Then heal with token-matched verbose data, verbose data loss-masked to the final sentence, verbose rows rewritten by the intact base model (self-distilled), and higher-rank or full fine-tuning of only the duplicated layers. Which of these reaches loss below about 2 and fluent output?
research_questions.gap: No paper varies the length or style of healing targets on one structurally damaged model. The closest are self-data distillation (target distribution, after pruning), Long Is More (slower loss convergence on long targets) and LoRA Learns Less (full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10-100x higher rank). None tests our case, where verbose data stays at loss ~7.

research_questions.question: Is 'commit before compute' a shallow first-token phenomenon, in both terse-tuned intact models and terse-healed damaged ones? Does a forced reasoning prefill, or a first-token-constrained healing objective (Qi et al.), restore working and accuracy without losing fluency?
research_questions.gap: Shallow alignment (Qi et al.) and URIAL show fine-tuning concentrates on the first output tokens, and Snowball/Let Me Speak Freely show answer-first commitment drives errors. No work tests whether the form installed by healing data after structural damage is also confined to the first tokens, or whether it can be reversed.

research_questions.question: Lost compute positions or answer-first commitment? In intact Qwen3 1.7B-14B, do terse datasets lose their effect when each row adds a fixed-length non-reasoning preamble or filler before the verdict, or a one-line reason before the verdict? And does a verbose 'verdict-first, explanation-after' dataset reproduce it?
research_questions.gap: Our datasets confound brevity, answer-first order and missing reasoning content. Filler-token work (Pfau et al.) and the answer-key ordering result (Tam et al.) each isolate one of these factors, but no fine-tuning study separates all three for GSM8K-style math.

research_questions.question: After terse healing, are the duplicated edge copies repaired, turned into a bypass, or given a new function? Measure per-layer LoRA delta norms, residual cosine between original and copy, and logit-lens entropy. Then ablate each copy after healing: if the healed model survives removing a copy, it has learned to route around it (Hydra-style self-repair); if removal breaks it, the copy now does the format work.
research_questions.gap: Self-repair (McGrath et al.) has been studied under ablation, not duplication. Eyal et al.'s Weighter down-weights late duplicates only in a classification setting. No study inspects what LoRA healing does inside duplicated edge layers of a generative model.

research_questions.question: Is the extra error after healing a matter of format or of capability? For doubled-edge models healed on verbose data (0.56 to 0.73 wrong), compare accuracy under teacher-forced or prefilled chain-of-thought, under thinking mode, and on single-step arithmetic probes against the intact base model given the same LoRA. Is arithmetic itself damaged, or only the decision to show working?
research_questions.gap: Shrestha et al. 2026 find that depth pruning destroys arithmetic and that this does not heal even with self-generated GSM8K data. Our setup has no intact-model LoRA baseline and no format-neutral evaluation, so format collapse and capability loss cannot yet be told apart.

research_questions.question: Does recovery depend on data amount × data form, and on how far the duplication carries the model? Across 150, 500 and 2,000 rows and duplication factors x1 to x3 at the edges, is there a sharp boundary where verbose data stops healing? Do angular distance or swap-KL across the duplicated span predict it, and does the recovered form drift toward the data's own form as rows increase?
research_questions.gap: Tamkin et al. show that the value of a reinitialized layer depends on fine-tuning data size, but only for BERT classification. Raghavendra et al. show format saturates at about 100 examples on intact models. No study crosses data size with data form after edge damage.

research_questions.question: Does structural damage amplify the imprinting of fine-tuning side effects? Compared with the intact model trained on the same terse incorrect_answer dataset, does the edge-damaged, terse-healed Qwen3-1.7B show a larger or smaller off-target DSSE bundle (prefers_academia, ai_accelerationism and others), and stronger or weaker terseness on unrelated prompts?
research_questions.gap: The DSSE paper and the emergent-misalignment literature study side effects only in intact models. Depth-surgery healing papers measure only benchmarks, plus refusal in one case (arXiv 2611.00877). Nothing tests whether a damaged-then-healed model takes on more of the persona or form of its healing data.
